At present those who are not regular civil service employees, although they may have been ten or twenty years in the service, if they are off two hours

or half a day are docked the time, and that is held not to be desirable. The minister promised some consideration.

subtopic: SICK LEAVE FOR TEMPORARY EMPLOYEES
speechtext: This is a question of long standing. Employees in the government service not employed on a permanent basis do not come under the civil service commission. As my hon. friend has properly stated, some of them who for a period of years have been employed on a so-called temporary basis do not enjoy the privileges of the permanent civil servants who are under the civil service commission. Under the previous government one of the ministers introduced an order in council to deal with the matter in relation to employees in his department. The order was returned expressing the desire that a fuller order should be made extending its terms to all departments. I have not been able to trace any further action in the matter at the time. I have had some correspondence on the subject with the hon. member who has just spoken, and after giving it some study have made a recommendation to the government. The matter is now being given consideration, and I hope that in a short time I shall be able to report favourably.

Yesterday the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) referred to the naval treaty to be signed at London to-morrow. With the permission of the house I should like to reply to my hon. friend in the form of a statement which has been prepared, and which sets forth the essential features of the matter.
As a result of the naval conference which has been sitting in London since the beginning of December last, it is now proposed to sign a new naval treaty to-morrow, Wednesday, March 25.
The present conference was convened, and the government designated a representative, the high commissioner in London, to attend, because article 23 of the London naval treaty, 1930, which was signed for Canada by Colonel J. L. Ralston and Mr. Philippe Roy, April 22, 1930, required such a conference to 'meet in 1935 to frame a new treaty to replace and carry out the purposes of that industry. A further reason was that, Japan -having in 1934 given notice of termination of the Washington naval treaty of 1922, article 23 of that treaty required the contracting powers to meet in conference within one year.

Unemployment
Ja,pan having withdrawn from the present conference, and Italy having indicated that she is not yet ready to sign, the new treaty is to be signed this week only on behalf of His Majesty the King, the President of the United States, and the President of France, The hope is entertained that all other naval powers will accede later with or without amendments.
The 1922 and 1930 treaties expire on Decern-ber 31, 1936, and the object of the present conference is to preserve as much of them as possible.
An outstanding feature of those treaties was that they achieved an important measure of quantitative limitation, that is to say, a limitation of the total tonnage of the capital ships and certain ships of other categories in each of the navies concerned. Unfortunately as statements given out by the conference have already made clear, it became impossible to maintain this feature. There are two main features upon which the conference has made progress and which are expected to be embodied in the new treaty. The first concerns qualitative limitation, that is to say, a limitation of the tonnage and gun calibres of individual ships of certain categories. The second provides for advance notification of annual building programs and exchange of information as among the signatory powers. These it may be hoped will afford a safeguard against surprises in respect of new or revolutionary types of ships or of unusual building programs. It is expected that the treaty will be signed by the high commissioner on behalf of Canada, and as soon as the text arrives a copy will be laid on the table.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):

It is an obligation which is intended to relieve the countries concerned of what otherwise might be in the nature of a surprise or a burden.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, March 23, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Rogers-Mr. Bothwell in the chair:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting relief for unemployment and assistance for agricultural settlement and rehabilitation and development of natural and other resources, and to provide for such payments out of the consolidated revenue fund as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour):	When the house was in committee on this resolution yesterday the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) objected to the propriety of our discussion on two grounds. His first ground of objection was that no intimation had been given that this resolution would be taken up yesterday. We recognized the soundness of that objection and did not proceed with the discussion. His other ground of objection was that the resolution itself was not sufficiently descriptive of the legislation which it foreshadows. Following his suggestion I referred the resolution to the law officers of the House of Commons, and was informed that the resolution was adequate for the purpose intended. I gathered at the same time that the practice with respect to the subject matter and comprehensive nature of resolutions has varied somewhat from time to time. However, I took occasion to look up the resolution of last year which preceded the relief act, 1935. It is in the following terms:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting relief, and to provide for such payments out of the consolidated revenue fund as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation.
I take it that the resolution which is in my name on the order paper is really more descriptive of the legislation which it foreshadows than the resolution which preceded the relief act, 1935. May I also add that our desire in advancing this resolution was to secure distribution of the bill which will follow, and to bring it to second reading. We felt that there would be a decided advantage in our discussion on the national employment commission bill if members of the house also had before them copies of the unemployment and relief assistance bill.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
With respect to the first point to which the minister has referred, may I say that I believe the action taken by the committee is a sufficient answer. With
Unemployment

respect to the second question, I have looked into the matter slightly and I find that the relief legislation of 1935 was, with certain variations, a reenactment of the act of 1934, and that the 1934 legislation was, with slight changes, a reenactment of the legislation of 1933. As they may not be taken as guides in the matter, I would add that the rule has been laid down by competent authorities in the following terms:	The resolution must be
sufficiently specific in its terms to support any legislation which may be founded upon it. In other words, if it involves an expenditure of public moneys it must, of course, originate with the government and be preceded by a message. The bill must be within the terms of the resolution so as to warrant its being acted upon by the house when the committee has made its report. I recall that on one occasion I found myself in difficulty on account of not having made my resolution sufficiently broad and specific to enable me to cover all the phases of the proposed legislation contemplated by the bill founded upon it. The committee is perhaps entitled to some explanation respecting the matters to which references are made in the resolution, and this would seem to be the proper place to have the explanation. Once the resolution has been passed by the committee and the bill '.s introduced founded upon it, the time for explanations has passed.
The resolutions respecting relief for unemployment one may pass by, because it may be in any general terms that the government may deem desirable. But the assistance for agricultural settlement and rehabilitation was dealt with in a separate bill last year. It will be recalled that the matter of rehabilitation was reported upon by a committee, but that in the end the legislation was entirely separate from that dealing with relief. Agricultural settlement was dealt with separately. Whether the provision in the resolution involves a comprehensive settlement scheme or is merely to provide homes on agricultural lands for the unemployed is not made clear, and I suggest there might be some explanation given with respect to it.
Then before we proceed to report the resolution I suggest the committee should have a reasonable explanation with respect to the provision for the development of natural and other resources. As it reads, of course the provision for payment is merely in the terms of a blank cheque, if I may use the euphemous term so often called into question in this chamber. I take it from what the minister has said, however, that it is intended to impose a limitation upon the amount, and that it is further proposed that any expendi-

tures to be made under the act shall be authorized by an estimate submitted to the committee. That is what I gathered from what was said yesterday. That being so it seems to me that the language is exactly that which would be used to express the opposite idea. It says "and to provide for such payments out of the consolidated revenue fund as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation." In no sense does it indicate that the provision is to be made by parliament in committee of ways and means, or when estimates have been submitted, dealing with the matter either by way of supplementary estimates or in the form of a bill fixing the amount to be expended, subject to the conditions mentioned yesterday by the hon. member.
In view of the statement made by the hon. member with reference to the law officers I have no desire to press the matter beyond saying that if the bill departs from the terms of the resolution, then certainly the bill founded upon the resolution would be in a most precarious position. It will be recalled that on one occasion that did happen in this chamber; when in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden attention was directed to what had happened, debate was suspended and the committee proceeded to pass a resolution so that the bill might be properly before the chamber.

It seems to me there must be some object in having a bill introduced by resolution; surely there must be some purpose in our having resolutions placed

Unemployment
*before us. We are getting into the habit of permitting the minister to give only a sketchy and inadequate idea as to what a resolution may mean. If we are not to have some explanation, why do we spend any time on this stage of the proceedings? May I ask the minister to give hon. members some idea as to the relationship which would exist between the national employment commission and this unemployment scheme? A few days a.go when the measure to establish an employment commission was under consideration I asked whether its duties wefe to be administrative or merely supervisory, but I received a vague answer. I suggest the minister give some indication as to the relationship between the administration under this resolution and the bill founded upon it setting forth the details, and the commission which is to be set up.
I have one other observation to make which is somewhat along the lines of the comments of the leader of the opposition. I do think we ought to have some idea as to what is meant by the development of natural and other resources. Does it mean that we are going into mining? What are the limitations? Are all these enterprises to be administered by one department? These are questions which naturally arise in connection with a resolution such as the one before the committee.

May I direct
my observations to the first question the hon. member has raised, namely that respecting the significance of a resolution preceding a bill. I believe the question is answered by the implication which may be drawn, from the hon. member's last two questions. When my right hon. friend was at the head of the government I believe he spoke on many occasions about the habit which had developed in the House of Commons, namely that of debating a bill on the resolution rather than awaiting the introduction of the bill itself. The resolution is essential as a preliminary notice to the house that public expenditure is involved; it so to speak, gives double notice of what is of significance in that respect. The rules of the house never contemplated that, on the resolution preceding a bill, all particulars of the bill itself should be discussed or should be the subject matter of a general debate. The present administration feels that it will not only facilitate the business of the House of Commons but will effect a greater dispatch of public business if when presenting resolutions the explanation is limited to essentials. We do not wish to seek to limit the amount of information which may be necessary at
that stage of the proceedings, but we certainly believe that a bill should be before the house when we attempt to answer questions which can be explained satisfactorily only when the proposed legislation itself is before us.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
It has been interesting to hear the Prime Minister's remarks, but they are not in keeping with his actions when he was leader of the opposition. Naturally the group to which I have the honour to belong are anxious to know what is intended by the resolution. We would like to have it stripped of all its technicalities, and would like to know the position of unemployment at this time. Has there been any diminution in the numbers of unemployed in the last six months, and is there any diminution of the numbers on relief? We would like to know whether there are more or less people on relief than there were some months ago. When the measure for the establishment of an employment commission was before the house we were prepared to allow the resolution to pass and the bill to be introduced in order to have an idea of what the bill contained. But this resolution is in a different position from the one of last week to establish an employment commission; for it is more or less a continuation of similar resolutions we have had before the house in years gone by. It is quite true that this one is stripped of certain features such as the blank cheque and the peace, order and good government provisions; nevertheless it does contain within it the making of provision for people who are now on relief in the cities and rural communities. It is only right and proper, therefore, that the members of the committee and the country as a whole should, be given some idea, at the time this resolution is being introduced, of what the government intends to do in regard to the general question of unemployment. I am not at all interested in the technicalities of the question, but I am deeply interested in knowing what is going to be done for the vast number of people who are to-day on relief. My latest information-and if I am wrong I hope the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) will correct me-is that over one million men, women and children are on relief in this country at the present time, recipients of public relief apart altogether from those who happen to be recipients of private relief. That being so, now is the proper and logical time for the minister to state what the government intends to do in regard to the general unemployment situation.
I know we may be told that the government is going to set up a commission, according to the bill on the order paper, but looking over
Unemployment

that bill I am sure no member of the house will say that it gives any idea what the government is going to do in regard to the unemployment situation beyond appointing a commission. We want something more definite than that from the government. It is quite true that minister's have stated during the last few weeks that they will reveal from time to time the government's policy with regard to unemployment in Canada. But in all earnestness and sincerity, I would urge uipon the Minister of Labour that now is the time to take the committee into his confidence and tell us, first, the exact situation in regard to unemployment in Canada to-day, and second, what the intentions of the government are in dealing with that great problem which the government have many times, in public utterances and in the preamble to the speech from the throne, admitted to be one of the greatest with which this parliament is faced.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word on this resolution on behalf of some of the larger municipalities. This government was in office from 1921 to 1030, and during the eleven years I have been a member of the house, I have been continually brings ing to its attention this question of unemployment. But what did the government of the day do about unemployment? Absolutely nothing. I have here the questions I put in the house,, the answers given by the ministry, and the debates on unemployment from 1922 to 1930. I took every opportunity of pointing out to the government what was being done in England and the United States to tackle this problem of unemployment, which had been made more acute by the discoveries of science and the application of modern machinery to industry. I urged the government to come to the support of the municipalities, which through no fault of their own were compelled to provide relief and hospitalization and many other services for those who had been thrown out of work, with the result that the municipalities got into a precarious financial position. It is not their function to look after the people in time of a great war, nor is it their function to look after the people in this great war of the depression. When the invader is at your doors, you are united and organize against the foreign foe. This resolution before us is just an expedient. It is a political expedient. This government did nothing to solve the unemployment situation from 1921 to 1930. As I have said, I have here the questions and answers that were given in the house on the subject of unemployment, and the gist of all the questions was: What is the government going to do to provide useful employment for the great body of unemployed in this country to-day? Mr. Heenan, at that time Minister 
of Labour, replied that it was a matter for the municipalities and the provinces. To-day the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) says the same thing primarily on introducing this resolution. But, Mr. Chairman, the municipalities are not going to be fooled by any such resolution as this. The party in power to-day criticized the former administration for its policy on unemployment, but what did the Liberal government do about it from 1921 to 1930? Nothing. They made a political football of the question, and when the depression came we had hundreds of thousands of unemployed. To-day a meeting of mayors of municipalities is being held in this city. Some of the municipalities are facing bankruptcy.
Personal estates cannot stand any extra municipal taxation, and any extra taxation will have to be put on real estate. The owners of real estate cannot pay any more taxes, and confiscation is going to take place all over the country. It is not a municipal function to look after this unemployment situation. The federal parliament is charged with the administration of matters relating to trade and commerce, banking, immigration, the tariff, bills of exchange, and so forth, but its first duty is to look after the health and welfare of the people.
The government tell us to wait for the bill. Yes, wait for the bill. Wait till seven politicians have been appointed to take care of unemployment, seven figureheads, like the other commissioners who have been appointed. Wait for the bill? The country will get the bill soon enough, in increased income tax for 1937, due to the useless commissions appointed by this government. We shall find our income tax rate going up ten or fifteen or twenty per cent.
The Minister of Labour referred the other evening to the late government as doing nothing for unemployment. Now he himself proposes some amateur interference with business in this country. How any business man can conduct his business with all the present federal interference I do not know, and these artificial barriers, burdens, and restraints and restrictions applied to industry have been one of the main causes of unemployment. What has become of the minister's promise the other night, in reply to the resolution of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), to study the question of youth and unemployment and the position of the industrial worker? It has been said that much study is a weariness to the flesh, and it must be so in the case of the minister. As Oliver Goldsmith, in his Deserted Village, said:
And still they gazed, and still the wonder grew
That one small head could carry all he knew.

Unemployment
It is a great thing to learn about unemployment and labour problems, but professors are not the practical-men who can solve this country's problems. I represent an industrial centre, Mr. Chairman, and I do not propose that this resolution shall pass without knowing more about the intentions of the government. It is all right for the government to tell us to wait until we get the bill, but after we have passed the resolution we can do nothing about it.
Here we are already in the spring of the year. Industrial workers were led to believe by the discussions that took place in this house that as soon as spring opened there would be some relief for the unemployed. Here we are housed in an eighteen million dollar building, and we can look out of the windows across the river Ottawa and see the hovels in which the poor industrial workers in a municipality in a sister province are housed; such a contrast and comparison. What is the government going to do for these industrial workers who are now out of employment?
Hon. gentlemen now on the government benches criticized the former government for its employment policy, but I say we might just as well have a commission form of government in Canada now, with a Hitler or a Mussolini at the head, if nothing is to be done to relieve the unemployment situation. We talked about a trade treaty here for two or three weeks that was supposed to benefit our industrial workers, and we were told we could not change a line of that treaty. If we can go that far in dictating along the line of Mussolini or Hitler, let us go the whole length. The man on the street is disgusted at the inability of the present government to grapple with this problem. It is true that our party did try to do something in its new deal legislation. We passed legislation to give the industrial worker a fair show, but the present government was in office for nine years and did nothing about unemployment, although I continually brought the question to the attention of parliament at every session. I have here the questions that I put to the government of the day and the answers that were made, and the speeches from the throne for every session. Every minister of labour refused to do anything. What did Liberalism do to help the municipalities with their unemployed? They would not give them a nickel. I brought up this matter in the dark days of 1927, 1928 and 1929, and I had the assistance of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). I asked the government of the day to give some relief to the municipalities, but they replied that there was no unemployment and if there was 12739-89
it was a provincial matter. The industrial worker and the agricultural worker are sick and tired of these commissions. With the exception of the hydro electric commission in the province of Ontario, I never knew of a commission that did any good. The other night we heard a debate on the industrial worker which I do not intend to repeat, but I think it would be more expedient if the government would appoint one man to look after this problem, as they did in the United States. If that were done, we might get somewhere. It is quite true that on the other side, they have not accomplished all that they hoped to accomplish, but they have made an effort. This resolution is directly opposed to the report brought in last year by the housing committee.
We should have a committee of the house on unemployment. Instead of debating this resolution we should appoint a committee which might get somewhere. What lias this government done for the unemployed? First, they offered the ambassadorial cure; from 1921 to 1930 the Liberal government created a great ambassadorial industry in the city of Ottawa to cure unemployment. Men were to be sent out all over the world to pacify the people on the seven seas. Second, they have offered an undersecretarial cure for unemployment. Now they are suggesting a commission cure for unemployment. There is one word that explains the whole thing, a word used on one occasion by the Right Hon. Mr. Thomas-it is all humbug. The people want to know what the government of the day proposes to do about unemployment. The onus is on the government of the day to solve this problem. The onus is on the Minister of Labour. Except when it was under the Hon. Mr. Gordon, the Department of Labour has been the most useless department in the government. This department has not protected labour, it has not protected the industrial or agricultural worker. The new deal has been sent to the supreme court and in the meantime the conditions of sweat shops and child labour, of the oil and other rings and all the rest of it are as they were before. Some married men are receiving only 87 a week. When these conditions are brought to the attention of the Minister of Labour, what does he do? He appoints a commission.
In 1927 I brought this matter to the attention of this house. At that time I quoted from a report of Senator Couzens who had been appointed by the senate of the United States to investigate unemployment in that couutry. A real inquiry was held and some of the brightest men in the United States came to Washington to give evidence. In 1927 I



Unemployment
asked the government of the day to appoint a royal commission or a committee of both houses to investigate the matter. The government replied that there was no unemployment, that the matter would have to be left to the provincial legislatures and the municipalities. On the other side they did not go as far as they could have gone, but they did make some effort to cope with the problem.
I do not know what the people are going to do. I see the hon. member for West York (Mr. Streight) in his place; I believe he will agree w'ith me when I say that many industrial workers will lose their homes on the first of May. We have asked the mortgage companies, loan insurance companies 'and banks to give assistance in this connection by lower rates but they will not do anything. Is this the proper answer to give the unemployed of this country? The provinces of Ontario and Quebec pay eighty per cent of the taxes collected by the dominion, and most of this money comes out of the industries of those provinces. Sooner or later these industries will ham to close up if they are forced to continue to pay these tremendous taxes. They are hampered still further by reduced tariffs and this amateurish interference with business. All these things are doing more to create unemployment in this country than anything I know of. The business man does not know where his position is. I know an industry in my own riding which was going to take on forty-five additional workmen, but when they saw what this parliament was doing they wrote to me and told me that they could not take on these men because of this interference with business. They have since released several of their permanent staff.
The resolution states that something is to be done to protect the natural and other resources of the country. The government that started the Beauharnois deal is about ten years too late in protecting the natural resources of Canada. This government is much too late to do anything for unemployment and for the industrial workers. The consolidated revenue fund is not going to be able to stand much longer the raids that are being made upon it. A commission of seven men is to be appointed with a retinue of secretaries, undersecretaries, engineers, and so forth. Direct contributions should be made to the larger municipalities where the great body of unemployed is to be found. Instead of handing out large subsidies and these cash votes to the provinces under the British North America Act, contributions should be made to the larger municipalities. The provinces come to the dominion government and make a deal, and instead of the municipalities getting

seventy-five or fifty per cent of the cost of relief, it is marked down from fifteen to twenty per cent.	*
I have sat in this house for nine years and during all that time this problem has been simply a political football. When the party opposite was returned with such a large majority I had hoped the government would offer some practical scheme to solve this problem, but instead they ask the house to adopt this expediency of a commission. It will not cure unemployment; it will not get one man a job. The proposal of the minister in connection with industry is nothing less than state socialism of the worst kind. Artificial burdens are to be placed on industry.
I have no doubt that the bill to be based upon this resolution will give this commission power over the law courts of the country. If a business man is ordered to do something by this commission he will have no redress in the courts. There will be no appeal from the commission -to the law courts, thus taking away the liberty of the subject. Down in Washington they have done something about unemployment. They appointed a committee in 1027 and were ready to meet the depression as we should have done years ago. I deeply regret that this motion which has been brought down in the second month of this parliament contains no practical solution for the cure of this disease. It will create more unemployment than ever. I regret to see that the municipalities are not going to be given some sort of direct help and protection. They cannot continue to do what they have to do under present conditions. This matter is a federal responsibility and should be treated as such. With the condition of affairs such as it is, with tens of thousands of men out of work, facing starvation and untold privations, suffering and even death, instead of the federal government assuming responsibility, getting things organized, and coming -to the support of the municipalities, they do nothing but write letters for relief lists. They have even written to the municipalities requesting them to count up and make lists of the number of unemployed, and that has cost the municipalities money. I am sure I do not know what good will result from the writing of such letters and the copying out of lists of unemployed for the information of the dominion government. I contend that this resolution should provide for some of the money to go direct to the larger municipalities, instead of giving it to the provinces. This is not a practical parliament if it cannot do something along that line, in face of the situation that

Unemployment
now exists-spring coming along and no prospect of work this year for the unemployed.
Last year the housing committee found that no less than $100,000,000 had been spent yearly by the federal, provincial and municipal authorities for the purpose of giving the people relief. The committee had before them witnesses including officers of the Department of Finance and the bureau of statistics, the gist of whose opinion was that about sixty or sixty-five per cent of that enormous sum could have been saved by giving it in work if a proper amount had been spent for the purpose of putting to work carpenters, bricklayers and skilled and unskilled labourers and so getting them off the dole.
The resolution and the bill which will follow it do not plead the cause of the suburban worker. Where does he come in? My hon. friends representing North York, South York and West York know what conditions prevail in those districts. There are men out of work or who will be thrown out of work on the first of May. The evening papers in the last three months have been carrying pictures depicting the state of affairs that exists there at the present time. Will these men have to wait another year for a commission to present a report? Why cannot this government follow the example of other countries, Italy, the United States and England, for instance, and come to the aid of the municipalities? Why can they not do something practical in the way of creating work for the unemployed by means of a reconstruction and building program, building municipal institutions which are badly needed, court houses, school houses, hospitals and other public buildings? Such a program could be carried out to advantage and it would relieve the unemployment situation by taking men off the dole. In the countries I have mentioned the governments have come to the help of the larger municipalities, bearing a third and in some instances half of the cost, while in other cases they have paid the labour, the municipality supplying the material.
I do not like to raise objections, but I see the industrial workers suffering, and when they come to parliament and ask for relief they receive nothing. On the bill boards in the last election all over Toronto you will find such legends as this, "Vote King and end unemployment?" Also, "Beat Bennett and bad times?" The late government did something material for the relief of industrial workers by legislation something practical for the first time since confederation.
J2739-89i
But this government is doing nothing to' relieve the unemployed. I suggest that this legislation be also sent to the Supreme Court of Canada or to that other court of appeal of this government provincial attorneys general. The minister speaks of studying various suggestions that have been submitted to him. I do not know whether he has completed his study of this question because we have not yet had a report from him. He promised to study the resolution in regard to industrial workers. Well, by the time his studies are over the unemployed will be sending for the undertaker and that will be the last of the unemployed, their sisters, their cousins and their aunts. No wonder the average man on the street is becoming disgusted with the system of government in this country-a system of the ins and the outs. That is all this motion amounts to; it is politics. We have been here a month and a half and this question has not yet been approached from any other than a political angle. I submit that we should appoint a committee of the House of Commons just as they did in England, and as I proposed ten years ago. There should be a parliamentary committee yearly to go into the whole question. The Ontario legislature appointed such a committee the other day and they have had a series of meetings with manufacturers and labourers and have urged a policy of reconstruction and housing for the purpose of getting people off the dole. I am also of the opinion that a portion of the $100,000,000 spent for relief should be utilized along these lines. "Wait for the bill" is the minister's advice. "Don't delay the resolution." Wait and see.
What are we here for? What is the purpose of the other chamber? In the time we have been sitting here, we have not yet had) a committee considering Canada's greatest problem, the problem of unemployment. The unemployed were disappointed in the first answer given by the Minister of Lkbour and they will be ten times more disappointed now. No business man will undertake to spend money in the coming season to put people to work with all this interference with business; he had better look out or he will lose his money.
This particular measure of so-called reform is one of the cheapest and worst amateur interferences with business ever proposed in a British legislature; there is nothing like it in the annals of quackery. No business man will be able to conduct business when this proposed commission gets to work. A commission of people who

have been party leaders throughout the country will be appointed just as was done in connection with the Canadian National, when they undertook to build branch lines to the sun, the moon and the stars. If that is the sort of commission that is proposed, then the sooner we end the farce the better for the industrial workers and the farmers of Canada, and especially for the heads of industry who are becoming sick and tired of amateur interference with business and of the artificial burdens which are being placed upon them.

This legislation, as proposed by the resolution before the house, is simply designed to give us that means of carrying out such agreements with the provinces or with industrial corporations, as the case may be.

I regret that I disagree with tlie right hon. the Prime Minister as to the purpose of a resolution such as this. The resolution is much more important than the right hon. gentleman would indicate. I felt that my memory might be at fault, so I sent to the library for the purpose of ascertaining what had been done in this house with respect to resolutions upon which bills were founded. I find that on the 5th day of December, 1912, the then Prime Minister, Mr. R. L. Borden, introduced into this house bill No. 21 to provide for the construction of three dreadnoughts and the payment of the construction costs out of the consolidated revenue of Canada to the extent of $35,000,000.

After he had spoken and the leader of the opposition of that day had made some observations the Speaker directed attention to the fact that this was a bill that should have been preceded by a resolution. Mr. Borden, now Sir Robert Borden, asked that the bill stand, and he gave notice at once that he would proceed with his resolution. The notice of the resolution that he gave was a notice in detail, setting out the whole of the provisions of the bill. It will be found that the resolution was in great detail, for the reason that I mentioned a while ago.
I do not propose to say more than that, in view of the fact that the hon. gentleman has said that the law officers of the crown have decided that this is ample for his purposes, because we will decide that when we see what the bill says, as to whether or not it goes beyond the terms of the resolution. But in his resolution Mr. Borden gave the entire details of the proposed bill, set them out, (a), (b), (c), (d), in order that there might be no misapprehension on the part of the committee in studying the resolution itself. He did not move the first reading of his resolution until the twelfth. He then moved first reading of the resolution, moved second reading, and when the motion was put for concurrence in the resolution Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved his amendment that all the words after the word "that'' in the resolution be struck out; the debate then proceeded for the rest of December and into the month of January. Now, what was the purpose? The purpose was first to elicit from the government particulars of the proposed measure, although they had been already indicated in the speech of Sir Robert Borden. The purpose in this instance is that this committee by questions to and answers from the government shall be in a position, when the bill comes before the house, to understand whp,t the bill means. Why? Because when the bill is before the house for second reading there can be no question and answer. No questions can be asked of the minister until it goes into committee, but before it goes into committee the principle of the bill must be made clear by the explanations made in the discussion on the resolution, not on the bill, in order that we may understand fully what we are to deal with. No one in this house who has a memory of what took place during the five years from 1930 to 1935 can fail to recall what took place as far as the then opposition was concerned. It will be recalled that on more than one occasion an amendment was moved to a resolution. A resolution is an .amendable proceeding. The great debate

that took place in the House of Commons on the occasion to which I have referred, from December 12 into January, took place upon the resolution and the amendment moved thereto by Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
I asked certain questions of the minister in charge of this resolution. I desire to have answers to those questions in order that I may be able, on the second reading of the bill, to have some appreciation of the principle which the bill is supposed to represent, because on second reading I am bound to confine my observations to the principle of the measure, not to the sections one by one. It has been held over and over again that any effort to discuss in detail the provisions of a bill on second reading is highly improper, for the reason that the details of the measure are considered when the house is in committee after second reading. The debate-mark you, I use the word debate as used in the rules of this house, not question and answer-the debate upon the principles of the measure must take place upon its second reading. How are hon. members to discuss this bill on second reading and the principles it is supposed to embody without being informed just what is meant by the words appearing in this resolution? I shall not take up the time of the committee by traversing the long detailed discussion that took place and the exact terms in which Mr. Borden gave notice of his resolution, even although he had then moved the first reading of his bill, and the observations of Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he moved his amendment to the resolution.
Now let us see what we want. I say that with respect to a measure for the relief of unemployment, we should have information as to the broad general disposition of the government on this question. They should make a clear statement of their policy, in order that we may understand the principles of the measure. How often have I sat where the right hon. gentleman now sits and listened to him fulminate against the government of the day for not having declared their policy with respect to these matters when just such a resolution was under consideration. Was it right then that there should be a declaration of policy? Is it right now? If it was right then it is right now. We have a right to ask the minister in charge of this measure just what he means when he says he proposes "to bring in a measure respecting relief for unemployment." He has no right to expect us to wait until his bill comes to the house-

We have a right to a declaration of policy. We have waited for it, and this house has been in session now for over six weeks. I use almost the exact words used by the Prime Minister when he was referring to similar legislation on a previous occasion.
Then we go further. " Assistance for agricultural settlement." The hon. gentleman has made some observations in respect to that but what is meant by rehabilitation? What is the policy of the government in respect to relief with regard to rehabilitation? I have asked that question civilly, but I have had no answer. Then next, "and development of natural and other resources." The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) has asked a statement of that, and it has not yet been given. We have a right to know what principle is involved in the development of natural and other resources in connection with a relief measure. I think most students of parliamentary procedure would say that when we ask for that we are making a very reasonable request. And I think it is a reasonable thing that we should expect some answer other than "carried" or " agreed to." These resolutions have sometimes been debated for days and weeks; I think the naval defence resolution dragged on for over a month, because the Christmas vacation intervened. I see one hon. gentleman before me who will recall it, although he was not then in the house.
Then we come to the next point, "and to provide for such payments out of the consolidated revenue fund as may be necessary. . . " That is a very simple matter, and the hon. gentleman has made an adequate explanation; he says it is to be charged against the consolidated revenue fund! But the charging against the consolidated revenue fund must be preceded by an estimate which will be subject to the control of this parliament when it votes supply, as when it votes supply in any other instance. So it narrows itself down simply to an expression of the policy of the government with respect to relief, what is meant by rehabilitation and these other matters to which reference has been made, and, further, what is meant by these very important words, "development of natural and other resources."
Further the hon. gentleman said last evening that it is proposed to ask the approval of the governor in council with respect to this. But more, he says it is proposed that the House of Commons shall express its approval or disapproval in regard to the various measures to be taken. The House of Commons obviously cannot do that unless all the plans are submitted to it before prorogation, or unless we do it after everything else has been done; but subsequent approval is not approval at all, it is merely ratification of what has been done by the government majority. We are entitled to a clear cut explanation with respect to what is meant by that as well as the other matters that the minister has mentioned.

May I say a word respecting my right hon. friend's attitude towards the resolution. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has cited one instance where my right hon. friend when leading the government directed the attention of the opposition to the fact that a resolution was simply a preliminary step in the introduction of a bill, and that the debate on the subject matter should take place only after the bill was introduced. I could cite a dozen instances where my right hon. friend pointed out exactly what has been cited in this instance.
I wish to speak more particularly with regard to his reference to the debate which took place in this chamber many years ago on the proposed contribution of dreadnoughts, at a time when the naval bill was under discussion. No example could better illustrate what I believe the committee will see as the true significance of the resolution. If it is the intention of an opposition to oppose in its entirety a measure which may be introduced, the opposition will naturally begin to oppose at the earliest possible

Unemployment
stage and exert all its powers to frustrate the introduction of the measure. That was so in the example to which my right hon. friend has referred. The Conservative gr v-ernment of the day was proposing to make a contribution of dreadnoughts to the British navy. The Liberal opposition thought that whatever was to be done by way of cooperation in the naval service should be done in a different manner, and should not be in the nature of a direct contribution. When the resolution was introduced the opposition of the day naturally began to oppose it at that stage. My right hon. friend has stated that the resolution was afterwards redrafted and details were set forth, but before making that statement he also intimated that the bill itself had been introduced, consequently all provisions therein were then familiar to the house.
My right hon. friend took exception to the Liberal opposition of the last parliament debating at great length a certain resolution which was before the house. The opposition was proceeding at that time with respect to the legislation of the government of my right hon. friend on the very lines followed by the opposition of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's day with respect to the naval bill. The bill to be based on the resolution made provision for a blank cheque. We were opposed altogether to the idea of a blank cheque, opposed from start to finish. When my right hon. friend indicated in the resolution that he intended to ask the House of Commons to give him a blank cheque, the opposition of the day put up as strong a fight as possible in the debate on the resolution itself. That was done because we were opposed to the purpose behind the resolution. Had it been an ordinary measure or one which did not involve a departure from parliamentary practice and procedure, we would in all probability have accepted it.
The right hon. gentleman waxed eloquent when asking the question as to how possibly the house is to find out the principle of a bill unless the principle is indicated on the resolution. I ask him this:	How does the
house find out the principle of all bills which are not introduced by way of resolution? Resolutions precede only a certain type of bills. He knows better than anyone else that the principle of a bill is discoverable on the reading of the bill itself.
In respect to the bill founded on this resolution, may I say that it will not be found to contain what might be termed money sections. I am not at all sure that
the bill might not have been appropriately introduced without a resolution. My right hon. friend turns to the past for support of what he has said. I have in my hand the report of a decision given by Mr. Speaker on January 16, 1912, which is as follows:
A bill which does not involve a direct expenditure of money and confers upon the government a power for the exercise of which public moneys will have to be voted by parliament is not a money bill, and no resolution is necessary as a condition precedent to its introduction.
Had the government wished to stand on the niceties and exactitudes of the situation it might have introduced the bill without first presenting a resolution. As the minister has already explained, hon. members will see when the bill itself is before them, that one of its sections makes provision that the expenses incurred thereunder are to be met out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose, and that expenditures, which grow out of agreements made under the measure, can be incurred only after the agreements themselves have been approved by parliament.

Some of the provisions of that bill gave the government of the day the opportunity of drawing on the public treasury for any sums without any appropriation by parliament. Let me read one or two sections of the bill founded upon the resolution I have quoted:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may, upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon,-enter into agreements with any of the provinces respecting relief measures

therein; grant financial assistance to any province and to Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited by way of loan, advance, guarantee or otherwise; and in respect of such loans, advances and guarantees, may accept such security, enter into such agreements and generally do all such acts and things as the governor in council may deem necessary and expedient in the public interest.
And also this section:
In addition to the powers conferred under the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may, when parliament is not in session, take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to maintain, within the competence of parliament, peace, order and good government throughout Canada; and at all times take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect and maintain the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof.
Powers the like of which had never been asked of or granted by any parliament in any part of the British empire at any time! Yet a resolution much less adequate than the one that is now presented was presented by my right hon. friend's government when he was in office as sufficient and ample for the purpose which the bill was intended to serve.
I think the procedure which the government has adopted at the present time has been in every respect in keeping with parliamentary practice and procedure. May I repeat, because I think in this my right hon. friend was right at the time-the unfortunate thing about him, as those who are not familiar with him will soon find out, is that he changes his attitude from time to time and from circumstance to circumstance; he does not stay in the same place with regard to any one thing-he was right when he said that the proper method of procedure in legislating, where a bill was preceded by a resolution, was to have the real discussion on the bill itself. But then he was speaking as Prime Minister, with the responsibility of government. He was taking the line which was the right and proper one. In that particular I am prepared to follow him at this time, although not in many others.

right hon. gentleman is an authority on that. I know of no one who can work himself up so rapidly as the right hon. gentleman to a point that becomes an ecstasy, about any matter that appeals to him at the moment.
Point number two. He says it was not necessary for him to introduce this resolution at all, that the government might have gone forward without introducing a resolution. Answer: But you did. Therefore the resolution is before us. What is the good of saying what you might not have done when you have done it? We are considering what you did, not what you might have done. That is that.
Point number three. The resolution that was introduced in the House of Commons last year by Mr. Gordon, then Minister of Labour, and which preceded the bill based upon it, was a very vague resolution, broad and general in its terms. Why? Because it was proposed to reenact the relief aet of the preceding year, with certain changes. But when the resolution upon which these relief measures were predicated was before the house, it was very fully discussed, and that will continue, I take it, to be the practice in all parliaments when the legislation involves a departure from presently established plans or principles.
Point number four. The right hon. gentleman suggests that the debate that took place in connection with the resolution about the dreadnoughts was of the character it was because it was proposed to oppose the legislation from its inception. But the amazing feature is that when the bill was introduced by Mr. Borden, it was not Sir Wilfrid Laurier, it was the Speaker who intervened to declare, without anybody raising the point, that the bill should have been preceded by a resolution, and when the opportunity thus presented itself the then leader of the opposition, as you will find from the records, let the resolution go through practically without discussion. There was some slight discussion on the first and second readings of the resolution, but when the motion was made that the resolution be concurred in he declared then his

Unemployment
policy with respect to it, because it had been pointed out by Mr. Borden that the resolution of which he was giving notice was a resolution that was in terms the bill that he proposed to introduce as Bill No. 21.
It will be found that opposition to resolutions is not always predicated upon the assumption that the opposition proposes to controvert from its inception the position taken by the government. It rather depends upon the subject matter itself. That will be found, I think, to have been the course of debate during all the years. Resolutions sometimes are vague and general in their terms. Sometimes they are very specific. I myself encountered great difficulty on one occasion when I introduced a resolution that was thought to be not sufficiently ample when I took it to the clerk at the table, and I had to redraft it in order to meet the situation in its entirety. Where it is new legislation involving the expression of a new policy on the part of the government it has been the practice to detail in the resolution the legislation which it is proposed to enact.
The next point is the point made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) as to what was said by myself as leader of the government in connection with the practice that had grown up of having a general debate on resolutions. What I said on that occasion I still say is correct, namely, that the debate should not wander over the whole field of discussion. I pointed out, as the house will see if it will be kind enough to look up what was said in connection with this matter and on a previous occasion, that the tendency had been to discuss everything on a resolution dealing with relief matters. I will give you an illustration. The then member for Kenora-Rainy River, Mr. Heenan, was in the habit, when any resolution dealing with relief matters came before the house, to embark on a general discussion. That is not the purpose of a resolution. The purpose of a resolution, once it gets before the committee of the whole, is to enable members to ask questions and receive answers. Important legislation involving public expenditures is preceded by a resolution and being preceded by a resolution, an opportunity is afforded when the house is in committee on the resolution to ask questions and receive answers before the bill itself is before the house. There is no experienced member of parliament who does not remember that I said then that the practice which had grown up of having general debates on resolutions was unsound. I was then dealing with a resolution covering a measure to establish an employment and social insurance commission. The resolution was not vague and general in its terms; it read:
That it is expedient to introduce a hill to establish an employment and' social insurance commission-
That is one statement, that a commission is to be established. The next statement is:
-to provide for a national employment service-
No explanation could be given of that; it meant just what it said. The next statement is:
-for insurance against unemployment-
That is a clear statement. Next:
-for aid to unemployed persons-
That is another statement. And:
-and for other forms of social insurance and security, and for purposes related thereto; and to provide for such contributions as may be necessary to carry into effect the proposed legislation.
I said then, as I say now to this committee, that that statement contained a clear indication of what the measure proposed to do and that I could give no clearer exposition of the principles of the measure than were contained in the resolution itself. But I was always available, for answering questions that might be asked. The habit, however, has grown up of discussing matters outside the terms of resolutions, of going into the whole field. This was the practice of Mr. Heenan and some others who are still in the house I claimed that that was not within the general practice of the House of Commons in dealing with resolutions. From that stand1 I have not in any sense receded nor do I propose to do so. I am gratified to think that the right hon. gentleman now accepts the views which I then held. It would have been so much nicer if he had expressed his approval in those days when under the stress and strain of office a little approval would have been useful, but he now accepts that as being a sound exposition of the law and practice and procedure of parliament.
I have not receded from that position in the least. If hon. members will compare the resolution now before the committee with the one being dealt with at that time, I think they will agree that it is not unfair to ask that there should be some statement of the principle which the government proposes to adopt with respect to the relief of unemployment. That is what we ask. Is that unfair? The hon. gentleman says that he proposes to make his speech on the second reading of another bill. He knows better than I that questions cannot be asked on the second reading of a

anoe for agricultural settlement and rehabilitation anu development of natural and other resources? What are the principles governing the proposals of the government with respect to relief for unemployment and assistance for agricultural settlement and rehabilitation? 1 do not think that is unfair; it comes wholly within the proposals which 1 made to the house in days gone by; and if hon. gentlemen, now in office, are as astute and careful in following the rules of procedure as they endeavoured to compel the government then in office to be, they will see what the complaints were that they made. Let them look at those complaints; let them see what they did complain of and what information they received. They endeavoured every hour of every day to embarrass the government, and now because a simple question is asked respecting this matter we are told that we shall get the information some other time and that the sound principle is to discuss the question not now but on some other occasion.
Let me repeat to the hon. gentleman: The only occasion on which, before the bill is introduced, we can obtain general knowledge of what is involved, because it is now a money measure-whether it should have been [DOT]or not is entirely beside the question-is when the house is in committee on the resolution, and the questions we have asked are reasonable ones for the purpose of securing a declaration of policy. Just as the questions which were asked us, or rather imposed upon us in the form of long speeches in days gone by, were in my judgment an unsound and improper use of the procedure of parliament, so I say on the contrary that a simple question calling for a clear answer as a declaration of policy on the part of the government on this important matter is exactly the purpose for which we have gone into committee on the resolution. That is the reason we are in committee, and I think I have a right to ask for an answer to the question.

I am in the judgment of the committee when I say that I have not tried in any way to avoid giving any information respecting the legislation to be founded upon this resolution. The right hon. gentleman did ask me to elaborate upon the phrase "agricultural settlement and rehabilitation," and when I rose in my place to deal with questions that had been put by half a dozen members of the house, that was the first question to which I directed attention. It may be that my answer was not sufficient. If I remember correctly I told
the right hon. gentleman that under existing agreements with a number of provinces there was provision for relief settlement. I am sure he is familiar with that relief settlement scheme, and we propose to continue provision for that scheme.
Rehabilitation was the point I was emphasizing.

Yes. Well, the word
"rehabilitation" I take it really means reestablishment.
We have a measure dealing with it passed in the previous parliament.

Quite so, dealing with a particular area in the western provinces. That is quite true, and I am free to admit that the use of the -word "rehabilitation" in this resolution may perhaps suggest a redundancy; it may not have been necessary. But there were two specific schemes for dealing with the unemployed: One, a relief settlement scheme, and the other, farm placement.
Both now in force.
We thought so for five years.

"Relief works" is a term which admits of expansion or contraction as circumstances and careful study may warrant. If I may refer for a moment to a subject that has engaged the attention of the committee for some part of the time this afternoon, the formation of a national employment commission will, I believe, enable us to determine much more satisfactorily than before the type of relief works which should be undertaken, and will also enable us to develop a program which may be proceeded with or discontinued as circumstances may warrant. We are deal-

ing, after all, not with a static situation but with one that is constantly changing. We must as far as possible provide ourselves with the means of meeting eventualities. At the same time we are anxious to preserve parliamentary control of expenditures. I realize quite well that the leader of the opposition has taken the ground in the past that the situation was such as to call for a blank cheque, a power in the government to draw at will upon the funds of the dominion treasury to meet this situation. We propose rather to place definite sums in the special supplementary estimates under items which I think will reveal quite clearly the direction in which we propose to proceed now with relief work. The bill which will follow this resolution is, as my right hon. friend knows, designed simply to give us the power to make these expenditures for these several purposes.
I am free to say to the committee that this government has no formula by which we may quite suddenly bring about a liquidation of unemployment. I wish such a formula were discoverable; every hon. member wishes it were discoverable. We must proceed on the basis first of accurate knowledge of the unemployment situation in Canada, and I think I am entitled to say-and I refer to the point made by my hon. friend from Broadview (Mr. Church)-that in the past few years, whatever may have existed in the way of accurate statistics with regard to the unemployment situation in the municipalities, this dominion government has not felt itself under any obligation to understand the unemployment problem in terms of human values.

gentleman mean by that?

I mean just this, and I ought to be very fair in making this explanation: Heretofore we have had, for example, such figures as 1,000,000 people on relief, or
1,200,000	people on relief, so many heads of families on relief, so many individuals on relief, and so forth. But the late administration did not seek as a government to obtain any information respecting, for example, the age groups of those on relief. The late administration did not endeavour to obtain information respecting the number of years spent on relief by those who were in these various categories, nor did they attempt to secure any information with regard to the occupational classification of persons on relief. suggested a little while ago; no one could face this problem without feeling under compulsion to learn as much as possible about it. But I found that the department did not have this information and that the late government had made no attempt whatever to secure it-

Last January a census was made of employables as against unemployables, but I am sure I am correct when I say that no attempt was made to get a break-down of the relief recipients into the various classes I have mentioned, and to my mind that is of first importance if we are to understand the problem in terms of human values and if we are to try to attack it in a scientific way. It is of great importance to know, for example, how many of those on relief have had some agricultural training. It may be that we shall be obliged to carry out far-reaching schemes of agricultural resettlement. Only yesterday in the debate on the reciprocity agreement-

The trade agreement; there is nothing reciprocal in it.

I am not going into that at any great length at this time; I simply say that this question of agricultural resettlement is one that obviously will have to be given serious consideration in relation to the unemployment problem. I" have no desire to take up any more of the time of the committee at this stage, but I do wish to make it clear that I have not sought in any way to avoid giving information with respect to the bill to be founded upon this resolution.
