May I say a word in regard to the resolution to which my right hon. friend referred a moment ago. He pointed out that at the beginning of the last session of the last parliament, on going into supply, I had moved an amendment to the effect that it was desirable that the government should make known its policy with respect to unemployment at as early a date as possible. The reason for moving the amendment was that in the five preceding sessions of parliament the House of Commons had been obliged to wait until practically the closing days of the session, or the days immediately preceding the Easter recess, before any opportunity was afforded to discuss the question of unemployment.
At the general election of 1930 my right hon. friend took the view that unemployment was the great problem; that it was the most important of all the problems, yet notwithstanding the fact that he was returned to power on the ground that he was going to end unemployment and to see that all persons were put back to work speedily, in the years during which my right hon. friend was in power we never had in this house any full discussion of the question of unemployment. The amendment was moved, because the government had in previous years delayed and delayed, as I have said, until the Easter recess or until the end of the session before giving us a chance to discuss the question. My amendment was intended to direct attention to that fact and to point out the necessity of the house being advised at as early a date as possible as to what was the government's policy with respect to dealing with the problem of unemployment.
May I contrast that with the attitude of the present administration. We have taken the position throughout the country and in this parliament that in the long run the cure for unemployment, and the only sure cure, is an increase in trade and what we should seek above all else is to develop trade between Canada and other countries. Holding that view, we lost no time whatever in consummating the agreement with the United States, as a first step, and in removing obstacles to trade with Japan as another step. These steps were taken immediately after we came into office. We put the trade agreement as the first item of major importance on our program, because we felt and believed, that
the sooner that agreement was enacted the better. Now we have come to the second major item on the program; which is the legislation we are introducing at this moment. This is the first opportunity we have had of so doing since the trade agreement was put through. As a matter of fact, before the bill respecting the trade agreement was given second reading in this house the Minister of Labour put through the resolution upon which was founded the bill respecting the national employment commission. The present resolution is being introduced in order that the house may have before it, at the earliest date, as complete a picture as can be given of the proposals of the government with respect to relief and unemployment. We are doing the very thing we sought in vain to have my right hon. friend do when he was in office; we are trying to get all these proposals with respect to unemployment before parliament at as early a stage in the session as may be possible.
The whole purpose in desiring to have this resolution speedily passed is that hon. members may have this bill before them when the minister proceeds with bill No. 14, which is the bill respecting the establishment of a national employment commission. In the latter bill there are clauses which can be rightly and fully understood only in the light of what will appear in the bill to be founded upon the present resolution. That is why we wish to have this resolution put through as quickly as possible.

May I ask the Prime Minister a question? In view of what he has just stated am I to understand that the commission contemplated under Bill No. 14 is going to have to do with the bill to be founded upon the resolution now before the house?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour, speaking a moment ago, indicated to the committee that the commission would have advisory powers with respect to some of the very matters which are referred to in the resolution before the committee at the moment. It will not have advisory powers merely. It will be a body so constituted that it will be able to coordinate all activities of the classes named in this resolution from one end of the country to the other, activities as carried on not only by the dominion government but by provincial governments and municipalities. One of the weaknesses of the way in which the relief problem has been dealt with in the last five years is that in the main there have been three large spending entities, the dominion government, the provincial governments
Unemployment

and the municipalities, and there has existed between them no coordinating and supervising agency. As a result there has been no proper audit, and no end of waste. Through the measures now before the house, the government hopes to obtain complete supervision not merely over expenditures made by the federal government with respect to relief but over expenditures made by all bodies and, as well, effective coordination of all effort, in order to bring about the largest degree possible of economy and efficiency.

I do not wish to say very much at this stage of the discussion, but I should like to point out that to anyone not accustomed to the way in which we do things here who was listening to any of this debate to-day it would appear that the important problem facing this country was not unemployment but rather the question of whether there should be a discussion on the resolution preceding the bill. As I sat here it occurred to me that possibly it was a good thing for Canada that those on relief had not been listening to all this debate. I do think that what the country wants to know and what hon. members of this house would like to know is this: What is the government's policy for relief? What are they going to do about unemployment? Are they going to consider unemployment as it has been considered for the last five or six years, as an emergency for which they are going to give relief on a very niggardly scale? Is that the government's policy? I am afraid the Canadian people will not get much comfort out of the policy outlined by the Prime Minister a moment ago, hoping to overcome the incidence of unemployment by increasing trade. If that is their only policy it will be no more successful than the policy of the last government. They cannot succeed in that way. There comes to my mind the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) on February 25, last year. He pointed out at that time that the number on relief-I presume it would be at the end of December, or perhaps January-was 1,207,345. The figures for December, 1935, are 1,206,429. So there is, one may say, no difference, no diminution in the number receiving relief from the government in one way or another. The Minister of National Defence made this statement in connection with an amendment he moved, as recorded on page 1182 of Hansard of 1935:
That makes a total of 1,107,325 persons receiving direct relief under the Department of Labour, and if we add the number receiving

other than direct relief the total is swelled to the appalling and astounding figure of 1,207,345. I think, sir, this reply to the question I asked is ample justification for bringing the matter to the attention of the ministry at the present time.
Then the amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply on that date was:
This house regrets that, notwithstanding the specific promises made prior to the election of 1930, and many times since reiterated, and despite the fact that extraordinary powers to deal with unemployment have been repeatedly secured from parliament, the present administration, after nearly five years of office, has not yet submitted to parliament any defining or effective policy to deal with widespread actual unemployment or distress which continues to be Canada's most urgent national problem.	.
The opposition of last year, who are now the government, have had five years to formulate a policy in connection with unemployment, yet to-day we find the Minister of Labour saying that the government has no formula for unemployment.
No formula to end unemployment, not "no formula for unemployment."
I accept the minister's correction, but it is a correction without a difference.
Bring in your formula; you must have one.
A formula for unemployment would be a formula to end unemployment.
Deal with the resolution.

We are dealing with it.
The only formula the government have, if they have any, is for dealing with an emergency situation, but when a situation has existed for six years it ceases to be an emergency situation; it becomes a normal situation, and for it the government evidently have no policy whatsoever except the hope of increasing trade. But instead of trade increasing, trade is likely to decrease. I am not going into that at the present moment, but it can easily be shown that through the development of industry itself, making it possible for every country to become almost self-sustaining, trade will decrease and is decreasing.

There is nothing to show
that.

Unemployment

The hon. member for
Sherbrooke smiles, but he will not be smiling five years from now when under this policy we are in the same position as to-day, unless a war should take place, which is not unlikely.

We have heard these
statements for two hundred years.

Present conditions did
not prevail two hundred years ago; we have entirely new conditions. As I said at the beginning, what this country is looking for is some policy to bring relief to those who have been on this dole for four or five years, to give them an opportunity to take part in the social life of the country, to give them hope and inspiration and ambition to do something worth while. There is no policy outlined in the resolution. I have read the bill for the creation of an employment commission, and I find no policy there. Possibly it is an effort to lay the groundwork, to obtain the information upon which a policy can be founded, but as far as anything we have before us at the present time is concerned, it shows that the government have no policy whatsoever in regard to unemployment except that of continuing in more or less the same fashion what has been done for the last four or five years.

I hope this
resolution will not be long in passing, but before it passes I want to say a word in support of the policy of the government as therein outlined.

Tell us what the policy
is.
Yes; in a minute I will give the hon. gentleman the policy as outlined in the resolution. If my hon. friends cannot read it I will try to read it for them and explain what it means.

Put some content into
it.

The resolution
reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting relief for unemployment and assistance for agricultural settlement and rehabilitation and' development of natural and other resources-
The hon. member says "Put some content into it"; I submit that the content is right there and anyone who knows anything about the situation can realize it. For many years we have been in difficulties partly because we have not produced as much wealth as the 12739-90
country is capable of producing. My hon. friend says that the government have no policy; if the group to which my hon. friend belongs have any policy it is to put everyone into the civil service, but the Canadian people do not want that solution, which is as old as the hills. I commend this resolution to those who believe that Canada has natural resources from which to produce enough wealth to take care of all who are willing and able to take their part in the development of those resources. I do not see why anyone should have any great difficulty in understanding this.
Then, as to "assistance for agricultural settlement," surely the meaning of that is plain: it means to help people to develop wealth from the land by making it fit for production, getting it cleared and in some cases drained and bringing it into a state of cultivation so that it will produce crops suitable for man and beast. In addition to this, the resolution speaks of "rehabilitation." In both these expressions there is promise of help for those who have been the victims of what the leader of the opposition called at one time a great national calamity.
May I ask the hon. member a question? Is there any shortage of foodstuffs to-day?
Ask the man who sowed his seed for six years running and reaped no harvest. Ask the man who during this current winter saw his stock of feed going down and his animals without feed.
Is there any shortage of food in the world?

That is a question which is unanswerable. I do not think my hon. friend has been around the world taking a census. He can learn by reading the daily prints that people all over the world are dying for lack of food. Why? Because they did not produce it and were not in a position to exchange something else for it. The meaning of the words "for rehabilitation" I think is clear to all who have followed the history of this country in the last few years. The victims of that great national calamity which fell upon the people over a great area of Canada were compelled to move into areas in which they were not able to rehabilitate themselves, in which conditions were difficult and their going not always wise. The government is under at least moral and economic obligations to assist in rehabilitating these people and to give them a chance once again to earn their own living from resources under their own control. I know that to-day many

Unemployment

scores of thousands of men who were once well established, before nature interfered with their prospects, are waiting for legislation such as this. Placing this measure on the order paper has given new hope to many people who will look forward to a time when they may be rehabilitated, and when they will not suffer from a calamity brought about by weather conditions.
I find no difficulty in understanding the meaning of the expression "natural and other resources." I could not specify definitely what the other resources would be, but one does not need to be a wizard to see that at least in part the words mean the development of the great natural resources found in the land of Canada. Mines, forests, fisheries, water power and scenic resources follow. However, we recognize that land is the greatest of our resources. If the land is placed under cultivation and is allowed to produce wealth many people will find themselves in better conditions. I have no difficulty in understanding the meaning of the expression "to provide for such payments out of the consolidated revenue fund as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation."
I confess I would like to see the bill, but I do suggest that the resolution is clear. It is not voluminous nor is it difficult to understand. It seeks to provide for rehabilitation, and to assist in rehabilitating many people whose fortunes in many cases have been ruined by climatic conditions. It seeks further to provide for the development of the natural resources of our lands, waters and forests, a procedure which commends itself to the good sense of the great majority of hon. members in the chamber, and citizens outside it who will be called upon to pay the bills and who will share in the benefits derived from the legislation forecast in the resolution.

Do I understand from the minister that we may expect no more generous provision for the unemployed? I would infer that this legislation contemplates merely economy in the administration of relief, rather than more effective provision than we have known in the past. I understand that in the present resolution the minister contemplates legislation which will have the effect of maintaining measures which have been in force during recent years, I refer to farm placements, the payment of direct relief, and assistance in directions already indicated. Is it not the intention of the government to break new ground almost immediately and to attempt to improve the living conditions under which the unemployed on relief now suffer?

The hon. member has
opened up a wide question and I am not at all sure that this is a proper time to enter into a discussion of it. Some time ago it was stated that special supplementary estimates will be brought down disclosing the directions in which the government proposes to expend public moneys in regard to relief and unemployment. When these estimates are presented I believe there will be no question as to the good faith of the government with respect to this entire problem. I would ask the hon. member, however, not to press me for a specific answer in advance of bringing down the estimates. I understand his great concern in this problem. I assure him we share that concern, and that we shall make every effort to deal with it on a basis not of narrow economy but rather of what is in the best interests of Canada, not only to-day but to-morrow. There is a serious danger that in connection with some of our arrangements respecting unemployment relief we may forget to-morrow because of the insistent demands of to-day.

I thank the Minister of Labour for answering the questions I asked, and I congratulate the government upon having adopted the principles which governed the administration by the late government. The hon. minister has been good enough to say that under the provisions of the bill to be founded upon the resolution he proposes to adopt measures which were adopted during the last five years, and which he named, to deal with the problems of unemployment and relief. He states that he may adopt other measures to deal with unemployment, but with respect to relief he proposes to deal with the provinces as has been done heretofore, (a) by direct relief and (b) by agreement contemplating employment in public works and otherwise, which will enable the payment of money to people employed, which will thereby relieve them from the necessity of remaining on relief.
In the second place he proposes to provide for land settlement on the one hand, and farm placements on the other, as was done by the former administration, and he regards this as an important part of the program. He proposes to make direct grants to the provinces under such terms and conditions as may be found desirable. I thank him for the answers he has given, and must observe that at least they abundantly justify the action taken in previous days by the government of those days.

Unemployment
He is now beginning to realize that the problem is a little different from what it seemed to be at the time he was fighting an election, and may I further point out to him that when he states that the late government had taken no steps to ascertain what conditions were prior to the time he took office he has forgotten two things. With respect to those who might be qualified to go upon the land not only was an effort made, but it must be added that a successful effort was made to secure the numbers of those who were on relief in cities and towns, and the qualifications which would enable them to take up and successfully cultivate land. Further than that, the unemployment insurance measure was put into force. Three commissioners were appointed and were instructed to take a census, and if their efforts had not been retarded we would now have a census of the very important matters to which the hon. member now refers. The committee would have that information when considering the resolution.
I was amazed at some observations which the hon. minister, a student of history, made. He suggested that the trade policies followed in this country during the past thirty years had brought the rural population into the urban centres. He must be familiar with Morley's Life of Cobden, and with the statements made by every historical writer during the last half of the nineteenth century as to the industrial life of England bringing to the larger centres the rural population at a time when free trade was at its height, and a time when there was nothing but free trade as the fiscal policy of Great Britain. He must have read about the abandonment of the farms by the hardy yeomen of England, a condition which has been so well described so many times by historians that I shall not do more than remind the hon. member that if the policy followed in Canada in the last thirty years is in his opinion responsible for that change in industrial activity, it is also true that the country districts of England under a free trade policy were deprived of many of their population, with the result that vast areas were left uncultivated; and it has been the effort of the government in England during the last five years to remedy the condition even to the extent of paying bonuses for wheat production, and for the production of meat,-eggs, milk and other products. I mention that because it does not seem to me that it does the hon. gentleman justice to suggest that the trade policy to which he refers, followed by this country for the past fifty years by Conservative and Liberal governments alike, has had the effects which he 12739-90}
indicates, when he knows that the most striking example of all is what happened in Great Britain during the great free trade years of the nineteenth century.
There was one statement made which I cannot permit to go without joining issue and showing that it is incorrect. The leader of the government said that the legislation dealing with relief was introduced in the closing days of sessions or just before Easter, and that opportunities were not given for consideration and discussion. Just how' he could have made that statement without looking at the reoord seems to me to be somewhat difficult to understand. I sent out for the Journals of 1934, and this is the story. The resolution was put upon the order paper on Thursday, March 15, 1934. Mr. Gordon moved as is shown at page 182 of the Journals for that year:
That the house do go into committee of the whole at the next sitting of the house, to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting relief measures generally similar in terms to the Relief Act, 1933, but which also makes provision for payment of federal proportion of delayed relief accounts, if any, which may be received subsequent to the date of the expiration of said act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What date did the house open that year?

I will give the date it opened and the date it closed. The resolution was adopted, as shown at page 205 of the Journals of that year, on March 22, 1934, and a bill founded upon the resolution was introduced and given its first reading on the same day, March 22. The second reading of the bill was moved, as recorded on page 215 of the Journals, on March 26, 1934, and the bill was under consideration for a long time. Progress was reported on six occasions, and finally, after very long discussions had taken place, as will be remembered, about very many matters, the bill was reported as amended on April 13, 1934, as indicated on page 245 of the Journals.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What date did the house rise for Easter?

I am coming to that, and to the day the bill received royal assent. The third reading was given on April 16, 1934, as shown at page 250 of the Journals, but before that was done an amendment was moved by the right hon. gentleman which, after a long discussion had taken place, was negatived by a vote of eighty-three to thirty-six, and the bill was then given its third reading on April 16. It received the royal assent,

as recorded on page 263 of the Journals for that year, on April 20, 1934. The house met on January 25, 1934. The bill received royal assent on April 20, 1934, and the house prorogued on July 3, 1934.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What was the date of the Easter recess?
It was very brief that year, it will be recalled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What was the date?

I have not the exact date at the moment, but I will turn it up because I want to show that the bill was law in April and the house did not rise until the third day of July. Very early in the session the resolution preceding the bill was introduced, and a long discussion took place that dealt with every phase of unemployment and everything else that might be connected with it, remotely or near. I will find out the date of the Easter recess, but my memory is that it was a short one that year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps my right hon. friend will give us what happened in other years.

The motion for the Easter adjournment will be found at page 203 of the Journals, March 22:
That when this house adjourns on Wednesday the 28th of March instant, it shall stand adjourned until Monday the 9th of April, 1934.
So royal assent was given on April 20, and in between there was that Easter recess.
I have also before me the Journals for 1932-33. The house met in the fall to deal with the imperial trade agreements. As a matter of fact, the unemployment resolution was introduced again that year, relatively, early in the session, and although the house met in the fall it did not prorogue until the 27th day of May, 1933. The legislation received royal assent-there was some delay in the senate in connection with the senate not being in session-on March 30, 1933, as appears at page 358 of the Journals of that year. The house considered the matter first on a motion to go into committee, as shown at page 243 of the Journals. Mr. Gordon moved:
That the house do go into committee of the whole at the next sitting of the house, to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to continue in force the provisions of the Relief Act, 1932, until the 31st of March, 1934.
That was on February 21, 1933. So the resolution was introduced early in the session, and the bill was assented to on March 30, 1932, and the house did not rise until two

months after. Therefore, I think the right hon. gentleman was mistaken with respect to the two years for which 1 v as able to get the Journals.
May I also remind the right hon. gentleman that it is a mistake to say that there was no effort made to coordinate the efforts of the various departments dealing with relief matters?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say departments; I said the work of the dominion and of the provinces and municipalities.

The municipalities are the creatures of the provinces and not of the dominion, and I took the view, which I have never changed despite what the right hon. gentleman has said, that the municipalities have no direct contact with the dominion except through the province. They owe their origin and being to legislation passed by the province, and their representations to the federal government should, in my judgment, be made through the provincial power. If that be an error, I shall have to be responsible for it. But that is the view I have always taken. Therefore the provinces made their representation from time to time to the dominion with respect to the conditions of the municipalities, for their primary obligation was to deal with the creatures they had themselves created.
It will be recalled that on more than one occasion the matter was put in this form: The first organization that the individual in distress appeals to is the community in which he lives and its organization, because he relies upon his neighbour. And who is his neighbour? It is the organization, village, township or whatever it may be, that has been created with powers to deal with matters of that kind. If they find themselves unable to deal with it, they appeal to the organization, the institution, the legislature that created them, namely, the provincial legislature. They in turn make their representations to the dominion if the situation be such as to involve action by the federal authorities. That has been my view of the matter, and I still maintain that that view is consistent with the maintenance of confederation and the principles that govern and underlie federal union. Otherwise we would have a situation develop that would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to deal with.
Very early efforts were made to coordinate the activities of the provinces with the dominion so that there might be no overlapping and so that there might be economy in the expenditure of public moneys. If any hon. member will look at the figures I think he will see that costs of administration and

Unemployment
distribution in connection with relief during those five years were the minimum, a smaller percentage of cost for administration than was the case with the disbursement and distribution of any such sum of money that I know of in Canada. The late Senator Robertson, who really gave his life for this country, went west and east and saw all the provincial authorities for the purpose of endeavouring to coordinate the activities of the provincial and dominion authorities. There were great difficulties because some one or two provinces did not feel that they needed anything other than assistance or grants in aid to enable them to carry on if work were provided by public undertakings, and this provided in connection with railway work and matters of that kind.
There then came a later period when we asked the provinces to set up commissions because any effort to set up a dominion commission, in view of what was said to us and with which I shall deal when the measure is before the house, involved a sacrifice of what the provinces conceived to be their sovereignty. We dealt with the matter by asking them to set up commissions with which we could deal. Some did and some did not. Some commissions were highly effective while some were not very effective. With respect to the expenditure of public moneys I desire to say that we insisted upon three checks. I know of no other case in which the same effort has been made to ensure that the dominion should not be made the victim of exploitation. First, the account was certified by the municipality. Second, it was certified by the provinces. Third, before a single dollar was paid a preaudit certificate was signed with the initials of two auditors in the auditor general's department. If there were any case in which there had been either overpayment or a deliberate effort to take money that was not properly due, the dominion was in the position of being able to look to the provinces to reimburse any such loss that might occur. I do' not know of any case in which there were greater safeguards. I felt that we had safeguarded the public interests as completely as it was possible to safeguard them.
As I say, there was a pre-audit in the auditor general's department bearing the initials of two of his staff before a cheque was issued. That in turn was done only if the province had given its certificate over a responsible signature. That in turn was given only if the municipality or body concerned had given its certificate. If these certificates certified to what might be inaccurate or what might be an overcharge, the dominion was then in a position to recover by any steps
that it might think desirable any money thus overpaid. In one case where we discovered that such an attempt had been made we did recover an amount and the treasury was reimbursed to that extent. Other cases were brought to the attention of the federal authorities by the provinces where recourse had been had to improper methods by some of those on relief. It will be recalled that the provinces, through their attorneys general, took appropriate criminal proceedings to endeavour to prevent a recurrence of such incidents.
I think that is a record which we need not blush to name and the highest vindication that could be given was given this afternoon by the Minister of Labour. When the resolution was introduced in the days that are past; when it was in committee, not once, not twice, not thrice, but I think half a dozen times before it was finally reported, we yielded to the opinions expressed by the right hon. gentleman and placed in the resolution itself a maximum amount that could be utilized for certain relief purposes during the fiscal year. We also provided other safeguards that the right hon. gentleman suggested. We did that in the hope that it would carry the unanimous judgment of the house, but unfortunately it did not. The previsions with respect to peace, order and good government were limited so that they could be applied only when the house was not in session. I have but little doubt that at least one resolution now upon the order paper could have been dealt with under the relief act had it not been delayed until after the house was in session. But that is an entirely different matter which will be discussed at another time.
I think in his declaration as to what the policy of the government will be, the right hon. gentleman has cleared up many misapprehensions that might have arisen. I was certainly thinking that rehabilitation had something to do with the legislation of last session. However, he has made that abundantly clear and has given an explanation of the proposals he has in mind. I think he has made abundantly clear what the policies of the government will be. I compare, the demands that were made upon the government of the day during the last terrible days through which we have passed with the moderation with which we have pursued our inquiries, and I am amazed at the difficulties then present in the minds of those whose function it was then to criticize but whose function is now to govern.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not want to delay matters, but when the right hon. gentleman congratulates the government upon following his policies I must point out to him that in two very important particulars we are doing nothing of the kind. In the first place, in the bill to be founded upon this resolution, there is nothing which asks the house to give a blank cheque to the government. In the second place there is nothing in the legislation which asks for blanket authority to enable the government to legislate when parliament is not in session with respect to peace, order and good government. In these respects our legislation is as different from that of hon. gentlemen opposite as day is from night.

As the Prime Minister has just remarked, it may be true that in these essentials this legislation is not similar to what we had in this nouse in previous years, but in effect it will have to do what is done by the legislation dealing with unemployment relief passed in previous years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: May I point out to my hon. friend that if he will look up the record he will find that at no time during the last five years did we object to measures of the class that are enumerated. We never opposed the granting of relief; we never opposed any settlement scheme and we never opposed rehabilitation or other matters of that kind. What we did oppose was giving the then government a blank cheque and blanket authority to legislate under peace, order and good government.

I am not very much concerned with great orations or long speeches, neither am I concerned with what the government did last year, but I am concerned with the fact that we have before us a resolution which I think it is our duty to pass. I believe it is a step in the right direction. If the Minister of Labour had waited any considerable time to present the bill, I would have criticized the government, at least in caucus. I think this resolution should be passed and the bill brought down and carried through so that men may be put to work on the great natural resources which are beckoning them on.

This bill does not come into force until the first of April, the end of the present fiscal year. Let me say a word with regard to the terrible relief act with its blank cheque feature, which has been the sheet anchor of the present government since the 23rd day of October. That legislation 
which would destroy this country if it were enacted and followed is the legislation upon which this government has acted almost every day since October 23, 1935.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the only existing authority.

Parliament has been in session for the last seven or eight weeks. Did the government pass legislation to replace that act? Did they pass such legislation as an emergency measure, as they could have done within the first ten days? No; they used the peace, order and good government provisions-

I think the hon. gentleman had better revise that question; he is expected to know. Appointments have been made, and important charges upon the public revenue have been made; one was made yesterday. It appears in the votes and proceedings and is wholly inadequate, because it does not show that Captain Talbot's appointment is to be made retroactive at $350 a month. It is under that section that this has been done.
As from the time he commenced work.

Yes; it appears now that he is to be given a job to help clean up the camps, but it turns out that he has been working since February and his salary is to be retroactive from that date. And so with the others. This legislation was threatening the foundations of the British constitution, but it has not been considered important enough to repeal it during the first three weeks of the session, indeed during the first fortnight if the government had wished to repeal it and to substitute something else for it. They could have stricken out the words "peace, order and good government," but they did not do so; they accepted the legislation and have used it and will use it until the 31st of March. And now they condemn the blank cheque. What is the difference between the blank cheque and making the fund against which you draw so large that you cannot exhaust it? The difference is precisely that which in-

fluenced the late government in this regard; it is this, that with the blank cheque you do not hold up the lollipop for everyone to have a turn at it. Hon. gentlemen will find what it means. We had our experience with the 820,000,000 and we knew what it meant. With the so-called blank cheque, surrounded by all the safeguards which we could devise, there was no opportunity of holding up a prize for everyone to make a grab at. It may be of course that the provinces axe better trained through Liberal instrumentalities; it may be that the method to be pursued will be that pursued by the favourite premier, namely, to repudiate and then make a new bargain on the ground that you can always make a better bargain with someone whose contract you have repudiated. It may be that that will lead to some more peaceful arrangement with respect to the lollipop.

When I made a reference to previous resolutions I was quite aware that the present Prime Minister and the Liberal party were very much opposed to blank cheque legislation as well as to the peace, order and good government sections which were incorporated in resolutions similar to this. I was also opposed to that blank cheque legislation just as I was opposed to the peace, order and good government clause in it. But, after all, the main consideration in a resolution of this kind is what it will accomplish for the unemployed in Canada. The average unemployed person in this country is not much concerned about the blank cheque; he is not concerned with technical questions as to whether it is in order or out of order; he is concerned with what is going to be done to improve his condition. So far we have not had anything concrete from the government to indicate their real intentions. If I remember rightly, when the present opposition was in office a few years ago and brought in a resolution of this kind we discussed it a long time, for days-
Hear, hear.

-in the resolution stage, and we tried to obtain from the government at that time all the information we could possibly secure as to what their intentions were in dealing with the problem of unemployment. With all due respect to the present government, I submit that this resolution is rather different from the one which we discussed prior to the introduction of the bill with respect to the employment commission. One was dealing with a commission to create employment and the other deals with something, either temporary or permanent, which is to be done for the unemployed
by way of relief or rehabilitation. So far we have not had any inkling from the government as to what their real intentions are. I am anxious to know what they intend to do for the unemployed.

Shall the resolution carry?

I was on my feet at six o'clock, and I must apologize to you, Mr. Chairman, because I did not know to what resolution you had reference when you asked if the resolution was carried. I was trying to obtain from the government some definite idea as to what its policy really is in dealing with the unemployment situation. I had also referred to the fact that the Prime Minister was quite correct when he stated that this resolution was to some extent different from resolutions introduced in this house during the last few years.
There is an evident desire on the part of the government to hurry this resolution through the committee in order that we may have some idea as to what is contained in the bill. During the dinner recess I did not have much time to look up the records in order to see what the present government did when they were in opposition, but I did have time to look up the records for 1933. I found that in that session, when the then government had a similar resolution on the order paper, it took six successive days of debate by the then opposition before they allowed the resolution to pass. The opposition of that time insisted that the government declare its policy when the resolution was before the committee, and I do not think we should expect a change of front from the government just because they now happen to be sitting on the opposite side of the house. I should think what was good in

1933 would be equally good in 1936. A great many people in the Dominion of Canada are vitally interested in what the policy of the government really is in regard to unemployment. I am not speaking only of the unemployed, of whom there are vast numbers in this county, and in whose numbers there has been very little diminution in the past six months; I am referring also to the fact that at the present time there is in session in this city a conference of mayors representing nearly all the large urban centres of this dominion. They are vitally interested in this question; they are vitally interested in [DOT] this very resolution now before the committee, and they are interested from more than one point of view. They find that the burden of unemployment is getting beyond the capacity of municipal bodies to cope with.
I do not know whether the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is prepared to-night to make any statement of policy as to the intention of the government in regard to the relationship of municipalities to this question of unemployment, but I know that would be interesting.
I am disappointed because the government has not disclosed its policy before this time.
I feel that a new government coming into power, with the majority the present administration have, practically capable of passing any legislation they wish in this house, should have come before parliament with a definite, settled policy, not merely in regard to the way in which they are going to provide employment but also in regard to the question of relief. During the course of this debate it has been claimed that the employment commission which is to be set up will attempt to provide employment. It has been claimed also that the government will attempt to expand the trade of this country and thereby absorb large numbers into the ranks of the employed. But even if our trade goes back to the level of the year 1929, which is probably expecting a little too much, we shall still have vast numbers of men and women out of work, who will have to be cared for by the state in some way or another. In other words we must have something in the nature of a permanent, relief policy or a permanent policy of providing employment.
I do wish the Minister of Labour could give this committee a little more information as to what the government has in mind than he has been able to give so far. We allowed the resolution that came up last week to pass without discussion because we wanted to see the bill. Now we have that bill before us,
'Mr. Heaps.]
and the government cannot entirely divorce the discussion of this resolution from that bill dealing with the employment commission. I want to ask the Minister of Labour if he is prepared to give this committee a little more information, first, with regard to the relief policy of the government and, second, in relation to the policy it may have in contemplation in regard to finding employment for those people who are out of work at the present time. I would also ask the minister, when replying to these questions, to give the committee the latest statistics as to the number of men, women and children on relief and also the estimated number of men and women who are out of work at the present time. Then, if I am not asking too much information from the minister, I should like to know whether he can tell us if the increased grant given by the federal government to the provincial authorities has been passed on in its entirety to the municipalities, in all cases.

My hon. friend also put another question with respect to contributions made by the dominion government to the provinces. Let me say at once, in case there should be any misunderstanding respecting our attitude towards this problem, that one of the first acts of this government on assuming office was to summon a dominion-provincial conference to deal, among other questions, with that of unemployment and relief. A special committee was set up to deal with that question, which held sessions during the entire period of the conference. As a result of the deliberations of that committee certain resolutions were passed, favouring, among other proposals, the setting up of a national employment commission.
It was also brought to the attention of the government that during the winter months there would be extraordinary pressure upon the municipalities of this country, which were obliged to care for relief. After very careful consideration of the entire problem the government reached the conclusion that it would be wise during the winter months to increase the existing grants in aid of the provinces by seventy-five per cent. That was done. As to the precise measure of relief afforded to the municipalities under this policy I may say to my hon. friend that in the case of most of the provinces the increase by seventy-five per cent of the grant in aid- went forward to the municipalities, but it was not possible for the dominion government to insist that any precise proportion of that increased grant in aid should be paid to the municipalities. My hon. friend doubtless is aware that in some provinces some municipalities which are already in default are receiving one hundred per cent relief from the province, including of course the amount paid to the province by the dominion. But it was not felt to be desirable that the dominion should insist that for instance fifty per cent, or the entire seventy-five per cent increase in the grant
in aid should be passed on to the municipalities. In the order in council we indicated that it was our desire that the provinces should give due consideration to the requirements of the municipalities, and in the case of most of the provinces as I have said we have reason to believe that every consideration was so given to the needs of the municipalities.

Mr. Speaker, in an explanation given on the first reading of this bill I think I covered its subject matter thoroughly. Those hon. gentlemen who have been in parliament previously are, I think, fully aware of the conditions that have been encountered in the administration of our seven national harbours. The purpose of this bill is to bring control of expenditures on these harbours under the authority of parliament, and to make the accounting subject to the comptroller of the treasury and to audit by the auditor general. The purpose also is to make the management of the ports more efficient. It has been found in practice that administration by local boards has not worked out to the advantage either of the port or of the Dominion of Canada. The experience has been that whereas the intention was that these local boards should protect the interests of the dominion government, the administration has often had the opposite result; that is, on many occasions the boards have actually forced the government into unwise expenditures by promoting local sentiment in the direction of a drive on the treasury for uneconomic construction.
Another weak link in the system as found by experience is that between the local board and the Minister of Marine who was supposed to control the expenditure. The total staff at Ottawa which has had to act as contact with the harbour boards has been one officer known as the supervisor of harbour boards, and his entire staff has consisted of one clerk and two stenographers. The result has been that there has been a delay in obtaining approval of recommendations coming from ports. The delay has not been the fault of the minister, but is due to the difficulty he experienced in getting accurate information which would permit him to decide on questions submitted to him.
In the new bill we propose to strengthen that link by setting up a board of experts at Ottawa. At the present time we have three commissioners, the first of whom is an expert in finance; the second, an expert in engineering, and the third, who acts as chairman, a civil servant of long experience who knows the background of work at the harbours, and who is capable of dealing with the personnel and the business side of harbour operations. In addition to that, one or two business experts and two or three expert 
engineers versed in the service will be available to advise the board in matters affecting the various harbours.
It is not the intention to operate strictly as a board. The thought is more that each phase of harbour engineering will be referred to the member of the board expert in the matter, and that an individual will really be administering a certain phase of harbour work. This, I believe, is a desirable feature in that it avoids delay at Ottawa, or delays brought about by red tape in this city. Each port will be administered by a port superintendent, who will be a man of experience in the administration of harbour work and one who is highly respected in his community. It is hoped and believed that the port superintendent will have, with business men using the port, the same local contact as obtained with the local board,. By having a trained administrator many objectionable features of port administration under local boards consisting of men without previous experience in port work will be eliminated.
Another very important feature is in connection with the engineering -work at various ports. Works often running into millions of dollars have been carried out by small local staffs who had not a back-ground of experience which would enable them to handle work of that magnitude. By centralizing capital expenditures at Ottawa we shall be able to bring to bear upon these problems the best ability in our civil service, an ability which, I believe, is equal to that brought to bear upon any port problem anywhere. We can also build up a background of experience in -port problems. At the present time problems solved at Vancouver do not help in the solution of similar problems at Halifax or Saint John. By the centralization of the work those in charge of port engineering in Canada will have a background of experience from all parts of the dominion, which will result in a considerable improvement in port engineering.
Another difficulty has arisen through the various methods of accounting which apply. One thing we find in going over the accounts of the various harbours is that in many cases work which is purely of a maintenance variety has been charged up to capital account, and loans have been made against that class of work. In other cases we find that interest on the debt has been entirely disregarded. In every instance methods of accounting are totally different in one port from those in other ports. The books of various harbour boards indicate a capital debt of practically

Mr. Speaker, as to the general policy of this bill I do not think there will be found at the present time very grave differences of opinion. These seven harbours are to a large extent the expression of the local interest, energy, enterprise and civic pride of the cities in which they are established, and a great deal of the success in their operation in the past has been due to the efforts of the local merchants and shipping interests of these several ports.
That there should be some change in the accounting methods I do not think anyone can doubt, and the providing of a new system of accounting is certainly commendable. But in reading this bill it seems to me that those who drafted it have not taken into full consideration the vast extent and character of the interests with which they are dealing. We find that by this bill some forty-five statutes of this parliament are repealed, and a new board is established to take over the work of the seven existing boards. But if the minister-shall I call him the Minister of Transport?-who has charge of this bill (Mr. Howe) had very considerable dealings with a harbour such as that of the city of Montreal, he would, I think, in drafting the bill set out a clear definition of the area and extent of each of these harbours.

We are not in committee. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will allow me to state my case, and I am stating it now in order that he may have ample time to consider it even after the report appears in Hansard, because I do not think this bill in its present form can pass the committee without very serious amendments to its provisions.
The area and extent of each of these harbours having first, then, been ascertained and established by the bill as the basis of the operations of this new board in each of these seven harbours, there are two or three other problems that we should proceed to consider.
First, it is the intent of this bill undoubtely to vest in the crown in the right of the dominion government all the properties appertaining to each of these seven harbours, and I understand that the new board to be constituted under this bill is to have control and direction of the operation and management of each of these several harbours. Moreover, the bill states that this board shall to a certain extent be the agent of the government of Canada. If cases of tort, claims for damage and wrong, and actions for breach of contract arise against the board, how will they be brought against this new board? Does it assume all responsibility for contracts made by it as the board of the Canadian National Railways is compelled to do, or as the board of the steamship company controlling the Canadian National Steamships is bound to do? Or will such actions for damages or for an accounting or for the payment of indebtedness be brought against the crown under a petition of right? That certainly is a very important question which should be considered, and I wonder whether the legal advisers of the hon. gentleman have fully considered it.
I do not understand that this board is one similar to that of the Canadian National Steamships. I understand that all this property is not to be vested in the board; that all of it is to be vested in the crown in the right of the government of Canada, and I should like to know and I think it is time now that we should know who is to assume responsibility for the actions for indebtedness incurred from time to time by this board.
There is another provision that I will mention, and I am calling attention to it because there is no principle in this bill outside the general provisions which I will deal with generally. This bill provides that the members of this board shall be a law unto themselves. They make bylaws, bylaws affecting all the commercial interests of a great port

National Harbours Board-Mr. Cahan
such as Montreal. Those bylaws are to be enforced without being published in the Canada Gazette, without any publicity really being given to them, without the merchants and ship owners and dealers of a great city having due notice of them. They remain in force until such time as the governor in council may decide to nullify one or more of them. Now, that is not a proper procedure in a case such as this, and I suggest that on reflection the hon. gentleman and his associates will see the importance, if the bylaws are to be framed by this board subject to the approval of the minister, of having them reported to the governor in council, confirmed by the governor in council and published in the Canada Gazette so that all interested may have full notice of their purport and intent before liabilities are incurred under them. If that suggestion is to be carried into effect, it will imply very considerable amendments to a number of the provisions of this bill.
This board is not only a board of management; it is an operating board. In the city of Montreal, with which I am more or less familiar, it must deal with large shipping companies, with the two great railway corporations and with a large clientele of merchants outside these categories. Are there sufficient and adequate provisions in this bill to authorize such operations as will be necessary to an operating board, a board that is carrying on vast business enterprises in each of these seven cities from the Atlantic to the Pacific? I doubt this very much indeed.
This bill provides that the limits of the harbours shall be as at present constituted by some forty-five federal acts now in force. This Statute repeals every one of these forty-five acts on the day on which it is proclaimed. Every person who is interested or who has conflicting rights will have to go back and study eveiy one of these forty-five statutes, or as many of them as refer to a particular harbour. The rights and interests of private parties involved in a bill such as this are very extensive and of varied categories. If the hon. gentleman had practised law in the city of Halifax for twenty-five years he would have ascertained that by actual experience.
Starting out with the fact that there should be a clear definition of the areas of these ports, we find another provision whereby the extending of the limits of the harbours may be done by the board of its own action. That is contrary to every reasonable provision. Section 9 provides:
The board may, with the approval of the governor in council, establish at any time a limit in the waters of any harbour under its jurisdiction -
There is another provision somewhere that the limits of the harbour itself may be extended by a decree of the board. The limits of the harbours are defined by statute and their future extensions should be also defined by statute. Provision should be made in 'this bill for such extensions, either by statute or by expropriations of property. The extension of the limits by statute should precede the expropriation of property for that purpose.
With the possible exception of the bylaws dealing with the internal management of the board and the fixing of the duties of its employees, I think that every bylaw affecting public interests should be confirmed by order in council and published in the Canada Gazette before going into effect. In connection with rates and tolls, section 15 provides that the board may levy such rates and tolls as are fixed by its bylaws and may, with the approval of the minister, commute any rates or tolls so fixed. I think these rates and tolls should be recommended by the board, approved by the minister and put into force by order in council after being published in the Canada Gazette. Every member of the public who is interested should be able to go to some official document, which in itself is evidence of its contents, and therein ascertain exactly to what rates and tolls he is subject. No ship can obtain clearance from any of these ports until it has paid all the rates and tolls which have been prescribed by the board with the approval of the minister. I suggest that in a matter of such prime importance there should be no doubt at any time as to what are the rates and tolls in full force and effect.
I had not intended to refer to the several sections, bu't I do wish to direct attention to some of the provisions in this bill which I think should receive consideration before it is finally considered by a committee of the whole house. A matter so intricate and so important as this cannot be dealt with by a minister in committee without due time for reflection. Therefore I am suggesting that these matters should be considered and I trust the minister will find it possible to make some amendments to his own bill to meet these reasonable suggestions and criticisms.
Section 25 provides:
The board may allocate any portion of its revenues, after payment of the expenses of administration, management and control, to a reserve fund for the replacement o,f fixed assets or of plant or of equipment or for the retirement of debt or for any other purpose.
Should the board have such authority without the approval of the governor in council or the minister? Section 24 pro-

vides that once a trust account is set up the Minister of Finance may make disbursements from it on the requisition of the board or its authorized officers for certain purposes. As nearly as I can ascertain, the Minister of Finance may make these payments without approval of the government. He is not restricted to the conditions of The Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, nor is he restricted to any other condition; he acts on his own discretion and every other act dealing with the disbursement of public funds-these are public funds

I suggest to the minister that he should make it clear whether the aggregate which may not be exceeded at any one time is one million dollars or whether, so long as the advance is confined to one million dollars, it may be made once each month in the year, or twelve million dollars in all. I think that clause needs clarification and redrafting.
The vesting clause, section 37, seems to be peculiarly drawn, if confusion is to be avoided. It reads:
The corporations and the board are hereby declared to be amalgamated and to form one corporation under the name of the "National Harbours Board" which shall possess and be vested with all the works and undertakings and all other the powers, rights, privileges, franchises, assets, effects and properties, real, personal and mixed, belonging to, possessed by, or vested in each of the corporations at or before the coming into force of this act, or to which they, or any of them, may be or become entitled-
And so forth. I should like the minister to consider, before this bill is finally put before the committee, how that section vesting all these undertakings and property in the national harbours board can be made consistent with the fact that by other sections all

this property is vested in the crown in the right of the government of Canada. I think there are inconsistencies which show that this bill has been drafted very hurriedly and without due regard to the magnitude of the undertaking of which a basis is now being laid and without due regard to the multifarious activities of this board in its dealings as an operating body with the commercial public, the railways, steamships and others.
I confess that I have perhaps gone beyond the rule in dealing with these particulars, but I do think, now that the government is establishing, probably for all time, the new bases for these operations in order to achieve legitimate and proper ends, the legislation providing these bases and providing for these complex and multifarious operations should be drafted in the clearest possible language, because the board will be coming into contact not only with our own domestic public and our own commercial corporations, but with every foreign steamship company that operates in these several harbours.

speechtext:
As one of the members from Montreal I feel it my duty to take part in this debate. The St. Lawrence route, with Montreal harbour as its complement, is the main artery of Canada's trade, for without the St. Lawrence route and the harbour of Montreal, Canada would be in complete dependence upon the United States. We would not be able to develop our commercial life and the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec would have no outlet to the sea, while the railways to the maritime ports would not be of great commercial value so far as the wheat trade is concerned. Any law that touches Montreal harbour or the St. Lawrence waterway is something that touches the heart of any member of parliament from Montreal, and if I did not take part in this debate I would have to answer some questions which would be put by the business men of that city.
The Montreal harbour commission has been in existence for seventy-six years. It has always been an independent commission and the people of Montreal are very proud of its achievements, whether it consisted of three members or nine members or more. According to Sir Alexander Gibb there is to-day in the port of Montreal an asset amounting to over $53,000,000, and more money has been spent. In my opinion any mistakes that may have been made in the past could have been corrected if we had left the seven different commissions as they stand to-day.
I do not want to place this question on a low plane; there is no question of jealousy as

National Harbours Board-Mr. Bertrand
far as Montreal is concerned. We in Montreal know that Vancouver must be developed and we know that the maritimes must also be developed, and we would be very glad if on the St. Lawrence route there were many other ports like Quebec, Three Rivers, Sorel and Chicoutimi. We also know, however, that Montreal is the key position in relation to Canada's trade; it is the head of the oceanic trade, and whether there is a deep waterway or not Montreal will always be the main port in Canada. Mistakes have been made in the past; there has been competition in wharfage dues which should not have existed; work has been done that was not yet needed, for instance, in connection with cold storage and the electrification of the harbour railway. There have also been developments which should have been made in the lower instead of in the upper harbour. But there are no mistakes that could not be corrected in the future if each port were allowed to remain under the administration of a commission of three men.
It might be hard for a new member to have to take exception to a law like this, but I live in Montreal; I practise as a barrister in that city and I have to do with a great many people there. I feel that this law is creating great anxiety among our people. According to this bill the administration is to be left to three men, one, I suppose, to be chosen from the maritimes, another from British Columbia and the third from Quebec. To me this is a question of good business more than a question of a new system, and I do not know whether the government could find three men in Canada who are absolutely conversant with the problems of the ports in all parts of the country. You might easily find one in British Columbia, one in Halifax or a few in Montreal, conversant with the problems of their own ports, but to find three men absolutely conversant with all the problems of all the ports would be a very difficult task.
This law gives wide authority to the manager of the port, so much so that in my opinion he replaces the commission of to-day. Well, if the manager is practically to replace the commission of to-day, why should we have another commission of three men which will form another barrier between the administration of the port and the minister? I quite understand that this bill is the result of the report of Sir Alexander Gibb, but in reading that report I find many contradictions. The conclusion is that we should have a central commission; yet Sir Alexander Gibb admits that in France, for example, they had centralization at one time and under a law passed in 1920 they went back to independent commissions for their principal harbours, especially for Havre and Bordeaux. They have given their commissions so much latitude that they have the right to pass bylaws; within eight days they must send copies of the bylaws to the government, and if the government does not object, the bylaws become the law of the land. At page 15 of the report Sir Alexander Gibb says:
There is strong evidence that the commissions of Montreal and Vancouver played an important part in this progress. They provided a type of administration at least the equal of any that was to be found elsewhere on the north American continent; and notwithstanding mistakes, which no system can prevent, the developments under the two harbour commissions have generally been sound and economically justified. I am not sure that quite the same can be said of all the other harbour commissions, although their establishment at Halifax and Saint John, I am informed, preceded a notable change in the previous despondent outlook in the two maritime ports.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the port of Montreal has been generally well administered, why not leave that port outside the scope of this central commission, as I understand the port of New Westminster has been left out?
At page 29 of the report Sir Alexander Gibb states that the British Indian ports are a success; yet they are administered by independent commissions. This, he says, is due to the fortunate selection of chairmen and commissioners. If it is only a question of choosing the right men, why not choose such men both in Montreal and Vancouver?
Then at page 31, paragraph S3, Sir Alexander Gibb says:
Considerable latitude should be allowed to the port managers so long as their activities are directed to carrying out the policy laid down by the central authority. It is essential to avoid emasculating the local administration, since no centralized control can replace an efficient and active local administration, or the special knowledge and initiative of the local business community, both of which are vital to a port's prosperity.
It seems to me that after such assertions of fact it is difficult to come to the conclusion that we need a central commission, at least for the port of Montreal. At page 73 of the report I find that the trade at Montreal compares very favourably with that of harbours such as Singapore, Glasgow, Hamburg, Bristol, Sydney and Melbourne, all or most of which are managed by independent commissions.
The only question in Montreal is that of deepening the St. Lawrence route between
1418	COMMONS
National Harbours Board-Mr. Bertrand
Montreal and Quebec, and I Should have liked the minister to give the assurance that within a few years we would have a channel thirty-five feet deep by 600 feet in width and
1,000	feet on curves. It is known that in Montreal the members of the shipping federation have been paying very high insurance rates; I was told that last year we paid 83,000,000 more than would have been paid on boats of the same tonnage going to Boston. It would take about $30,000,000 to deepen the channel, and the work could be completed in three years if it were started at the opening of navigation and continued without a halt. It is common knowledge that the dredges belonging to the government do not work as late in the season as they should, and that therefore the capital cost is a great deal more than it should be.
