Why not spend on the channel at least $30,000,000 within three or four years, and charge it to capital expenditure or issue bonds, if necessary, so that we shall not hear of shipping men having to portage some of their goods between Quebec and Montreal?
Briefly, I do not think anyone can take care of the interests of Montreal harbour as well as can the business men of Montreal, or that anyone can take care of the interests of Vancouver harbour as well as can the business men of Vancouver. Montreal harbour has always been a business proposition conducted by business men, and I do not see why to-day we should depart from that practice and adopt another system which, I feel sure, will meet with many difficulties in the coming year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
Like the previous speaker (Mr. Bertrand, Laurier), I am very much interested in the port of Montreal. I recognize the importance of the subject under discussion and the value of the resolution introduced by the Minister of Marine (Mr. Howe). It was very gratifying to sit on this side of the house and hear a measure of this kind introduced without any reference by the minister to what the opposition had done while they were in office. That feature of the minister's statement commended itself to me and no doubt to other hon. members.
We have in Canada seven national ports, and in discussing a matter of this sort we should as far as possible forget the locality from which we come and discuss the question from a national point of view. I feel absolutely certain that in discussing this proposed measure from a national point of view we shall be working in the best interests of that part of the country which we represent,

be it an inland constituency or one vitally interested at any one of these ports. The previous speaker referred to mistakes made in the past by local harbour boards. We in Montreal have recognized those mistakes. We see the Montreal port authorities discarding electric locomotives and electric equipment which cost an enormous amount to instal, and going back to steam motive power as previously used. And greater mistakes than that have been made; to the tremendous financial loss of our country we have made national ports where local ports only should have existed. We have seven so-called national ports. To my mind we could get along very well with five. I shall not designate the two that could have remained as local ports to the probable advantage of the locality in which they are situated and the advantage of Canada as a whole.
The previous speaker suggested that it might be difficult to find three men capable of administering these national ports. Surely he did not make that suggestion seriously. Surely in Canada we have three men capable of handling that situation. I would pay this compliment to the minister who introduced this measure, that if he were not occupied as he is I would designate him as one man quite capable of taking a job of this kind and doing it well. No; we do not lack good men in Canada, and I hope that when this board is finally named we shall find that the government have selected three Canadians who are quite capable of looking after these national ports. In selecting these men for this important work I hope the government will not take into account any particular locality or any particular port, but will select them purely and simply for their outstanding ability for the job. I would not care if every one of those men came from Winnipeg, or from Toronto or from Halifax, as long as they are good capable men for the job.
One point that impressed me while the minister was speaking was in connection with the expense to be incurred. I notice in the bill this provision:
4.	(1) The board may employ such professional, technical and other officers, clerks and employees as it may deem necessary for the proper conduct of its business1 and' fix their remuneration.
That means of course a staff. A staff is necessary. I hope it does not mean increased expenditure as far as our national ports are concerned. I hope that the staff which is required will be drawn from those already in the employ of our local ports, and that none of those locally employed will be let out of employment by reason of the creation of this

National Harbours Board-Mr. Walsh
central board. I hope that this new board is not going to develop into another huge department of government to burden the people of this country with further taxation, but that it will mean a lessening of the amounts required.
The previous speaker referred to difficulty, under this measure, of maintaining or the inability to maintain the proper local contacts with the ports, with particular reference to Montreal. Of course there should be local contact; means must be developed to maintain that local contact, and I have confidence in the present minister and know that he will appoint to the various ports managers who will maintain it. I believe that the local manager will be quite sufficient to maintain that local contact which is so necessary if this measure is to be a success. I feel that his efforts will be supplemented and carefully watched by important public bodies in the communities so vitally interested. I am absolutely certain that Montreal's interests will be well looked after by the chambre de commerce and the board of trade and even the Montreal city council. The local manager will not be allowed to go far astray in taking care of the interests of Montreal without those bodies knowing something about the matter and advising the government of what they have in their minds. I know the minister will be kept fully advised by these bodies if the local manager is acting in any way detrimental to the best interests of the city of Montreal, and doubtless the same can be said of Halifax, Vancouver and the other cities concerned.
I should like to join with the hon. member for Laurier in urging that the minister bear in mind the importance of Montreal as a national port, the keystone of the commercial situation in the Dominion of Canada. As the port of Montreal prospers, so will the Dominion of Canada prosper. And the prosperity of the port of Montreal is not dependent so much upon the port commission in Montreal; it is absolutely dependent upon the depth and width of the channel leading to the port. I should like to ask the Minister of Marine to see that the channel is deepened and widened to the extent necessary to bring all ocean going vessels to the port of Montreal, and I would urge him not to do this by contract. I feel that contracts let by the Department of Marine in connection with the harbour of Montreal are of a nefarious character, and it is my view that the work of deepening the channel leading to the port should be done by the federal department. It should use its own dredges and men, and t'he work should begin as 12739-91
early as possible and continue as late as possible. In that way I feel we would get one hundred cents in value for every dollar spent on deepening the channel leading to the port of Montreal.
There is another feature of the bill about which I have not made up my mind, but for some reason or another I think I must say that I do not like it. I refer to the part which deals with calling for tenders for supplies. I notice that this matter is more or less in the hands of the government. I am always afraid of tenders that come to a government and are dealt with by the governor in council. I always feel that if they were left to an independent body, or that if these three men were put in absolute and complete charge and were given authority to say who should receive the awards for tenders we would have a square deal, provided we could keep these three men free from political contact.
When a government is calling for tenders I always feel that something is to be done for the benefit of the government in power, and anything which reflects benefit on the party in power is paid for by the people; we do not get full value for our money. I must say that I do not care for that particular feature in the bill and I hope the minister will find some remedy for it before the measure reaches the final stage.
May I commend the Minister of Marine for bringing in this legislation. I know it will meet with considerable criticism from certain quarters, and many people are going to look at it from a narrow and selfish point of view. I come from Montreal, a point from which a great part of the criticism will come, and I want to say to the minister that during my last visit to that city, no longer ago than the past week-end, among those with whom I had contact this measure appeared to be meeting with favour. They feel that if the measure is properly moulded into shape, and if many of the suggestions already advanced by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) are included, we shall have something of real and vital interest to the Dominion of Canada, and something which will place these national ports, in which we are all interested, in a better position. I do not care whether a man comes from Saskatchewan, Alberta or any other province, the fact is he is vitally interested in the ports and in their development from a national standpoint.
May I again commend the minister for the change which is about to take place. I want him to know that many citizens, even in the city of Montreal, are looking upon this

1420	COMMONS
National Harbours Board-Mr, Church
measure as one of salvation, provided it is worked out along tie business lines which they know the minister is capable of developing. I hope that he will not be unduly influenced by other influences or suggestions which might be brought to bear in connection with this important development.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a few words about the principle of the bill. May I say that the National Ports Survey by Sir Alexander Gibb is most interesting. It reveals a waste of money in connection with harbours. Hon. members will notice that none of the ports mentioned in the bill is in Ontario. Mistakes have been made in the Department of Marine, because after all is said and done it has been saturated since confederation with politics. These ports have not been built or operated from a commercial standpoint, because we know that many of them have been foolish political ventures.
I suggest that the late government deserves a great deal of credit for having brought to the attention of the country the report by Sir Alexander Gibb in which are outlined the mistakes made in connection with these so-called national ports. Then, the Drayton-Aeworth report made many years earlier on our railways problem indicated the great wastage in railway construction. It was pointed out that we had three transcontinental lines with a single track mileage of 40,000 miles, serving a population of about 10,000,000 people. Our mileage is equal to that of the United Kingdom or France, either of which has a much greater population.
Ontario does not benefit from the operation of the bill, although it is paying forty per cent of Canada's taxes. I do not object to the principle of the bill; in. fact, I believe if it had been introduced several years ago Canada would have been saved many millions of dollars in the construction of useless breakwaters and harbours. However, as I have said, since confederation this department has been saturated with politics. The first paragraph in the National Ports Survey by Sir Alexander Gibb is as follows:
The ports of Canada, although they have a capital value of about $370,000,000 only, are part of a transportation system which, including railways, canals and roads, is assessed at $4,500,000,000 and constitutes over a seventh of the country's estimated wealth. The principal ports are not, as in many countries, founded on the service of a great exporting or consuming area in their immediate neighbourhood; nor have they been created and developed by merchant or shipping interests. They exist primarily as the connection between land and sea in the long route that the exports of Canada must take to reach their market;

and for that reason, by the terms of confederation, and in distinction from the position in the United States where the ports have remained almost entirely in the control of individual states and cities, almost all ports in Canada have become federal property.
No doubt many mistakes have been made in the past. I do not object to the principle of the bill founded upon the report, although doubtless there are many errors in it. The fact is, however, that there is an investment of about $200,000,000 and there should be more direct control by parliament over expenditures. In the old days individual amounts were voted. There were votes for Halifax harbour, Saint John harbour, and the harbours at Chicoutimi, Quebec, Three Rivers, Montreal and Vancouver. In addition there was a vote for the ship channel between Montreal and Quebec, something which has cost the people of Canada many millions of dollars. As I have pointed out, while some are national ports, others are only political ports, but if we are to have a proper national harbour system we must have some control in the gulf of St. Lawrence, the St. Lawrence river and the great lakes.
Ontario has had to develop its own ports as municipal institutions. Toronto, from which I come, spent about $30,000,000 on its own harbour. Work which was done in other parts of Canada by the federal government had to be done in that city at the expense of Toronto's taxpayers. You will be familiar with the situation in Montreal, Mr. Speaker, where work has been done in connection with beautifying the harbour. The same has been done at Halifax, Saint John and Vancouver. I may say that I believe many of the commissions have done good work. They have been local men, and of course politics has been mixed up with the administration of the harbours. I believe that it is possible to effect economies through this central board. In the United States, the states of New York and New Jersey have harbour boards, and not only do they have control of harbours and. the power to issue bylaws, but they have a system which is linked up with state and municipal institutions. After all is said and done, that is where waste has occurred. There has been no connecting link between our harbour boards and the Department of Marine at Ottawa, the Public Works department, and our municipalities.
If we are to have a proper transportation system, this new board should also have control over the canal system of this country and over shipping and navigation on the great lakes. Shipping, of course, is not under the control of the railway board. It is under no

National Harbours Board-Mr. Isnor
regulation except the law of supply and demand. In my opinion, Bill No. 17 does not go far enough. It should include some provision to afford relief to the citizens of Ontario from the present state of affairs, in which they are called upon to develop their own harbours very largely, without votes from this parliament at all. Take Toronto, for instance. Although the federal government has two commissioners on the Toronto harbour board, the government of Canada does not contribute a nickel to that board. All the money which is spent on Toronto harbour and on that twelve-mile waterfront is city money. I believe that the principle of this legislation should be applied to all the great ports on lake Ontario and the great lakes, and power should be given to the board to buy out all these waterfronts, so that waterborne traffic may be given a chance in this country. So far it has never had a chance in this dominion in connection with rail traffic, and it is a vitally important link in our transportation system.
This bill is not perfect by any means. It will do nothing for the ports I have mentioned on the great lakes, such places as Toronto, Trenton, Colborne, Belleville and other ports on lake Ontario, lake Erie, lake Huron and lake Superior in the province of Ontario, which pays nearly forty per cent of the taxes collected by the federal government. The minister himself comes from the head of the lakes, and I hope he will give this suggestion sympathetic consideration. The lake ports in Ontario ever since confederation have had to do all their own work of deepening and dredging harbours, which is purely a federal work, and yet it has been done at the cost of the taxpayers of Ontario. What about life-saving stations in all these harbours and on the great lakes? The municipalities of Ontario have had to pay for all that themselves. All that Toronto gets from the dominion government is a little money for dredging the entrances to the harbour and for building breakwaters.
I believe that the principle of this bill is all right. Undoubtedly a large amount of money has been wasted in the so-called national ports of this country, and the people have not been getting the value they should have got in facilities for the transport of grain to the seaboard, in developing the coal resources of Alberta and the maritime provinces, and in developing the grain growing industry in the prairie provinces. In none of these matters have we got the full value of our ports and canal system.
Of course we have to consider the principle of the bill on the second reading, and I hope the minister will take into consideration the 12739-914
suggestions I have made. I hope he will consider doing something for the ports on lake Ontario, which are entitled to some consideration; and so far as the ports mentioned in this bill are concerned, provision should be made for helping these municipalities in the matter of parks, boulevards and driveways along the magnificent ports, for example, of Montreal and Vancouver, on which so much of the taxpayers' money has been spent.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, I must confess that like many other members I could not quite follow the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Church) as well as I should like to have done. I did follow the previous speaker (Mr. Walsh) with a great deal of interest, and I wish to compliment him upon the clear and concise manner in which he presented his views on the principle of this bill. I agree with many of the views he expressed, particularly what he said with reference to the Minister of Marine (Mr. Howe) who sponsors this bill. I feel that Canada would indeed be fortunate if we were to get a man of his type as head of this national harbours board.
If it were not the principle of the bill that we are now considering, I would take time to comment on one or two of the observations made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Bertrand), who referred to the port of Montreal, but as at this stage we are dealing solely with the principle of the bill, I shall simply say that we have in Halifax a harbour which it is not necessary to dredge, where it is not necessary to spend thirty million dollars in deepening a channel, and a harbour which extends sixteen miles inward from the sea, offering complete shelter for every vessel of any size. Halifax harbour is open the year round. The harbour is known as the eastern gateway to Canada, and because I represent the city of Halifax I desire to say just a few words on the principle of this bill.
The minister in the course of his remarks referred to the importance of the local view, and stated that it would be given effect to by selecting the port manager or the port superintendent from the locality in which the port was situated. I feel that that is an important factor, and particularly with regard to Halifax and Vancouver. The interests of the port of Montreal, which are centred to a large extent around that city, I feel will be very well looked after by a central board located at Ottawa, which is so close to Montreal, but I am just a little fearful as to the effect which this bill might have on the ports of Halifax and Vancouver. I sincerely trust that the minister and the government, when deciding upon the personnel of the new board,

National Harbours Board-Mr. Isnor
will take into consideration, along with other necessary qualifications, the selection of men who are vitally interested in the east and the west, because otherwise I feel that this new board will not bring about the results which we desire. I pass that on as a suggestion to the minister for his consideration when deciding on the personnel of the board.
In regard to more efficient methods of port administration, I have read the reports published by the two commissions which inquired into harbour development in Canada. The most recent one, prepared by Sir Alexander Gibb and presented to the government of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), contains many valuable suggestions and recommendations. I think the bill introduced by .the minister is to some extent along the lines of this report.
I would point out that the report made particular mention of the efficient management of the port at Halifax, situated in the constituency which I represent. I believe that local management will develop more efficiency in one particular than will a central board. I have in mind the developing of trade for a particular port. I believe that a local board is more apt to bring about better results and provide more efficient management than will be this so-called long-armed control. I am just a little fearful as to how the two ports of Vancouver and Halifax will be affected.
The minister referred to unwise expenditure, but let me say that that is not the fault of the managements of the various ports. That matter rested with the minister under whom the harbour commissions operated. As I understand the situation, it was necessary for the various harbour boards to obtain permission and approval before they could make any expenditure. If that is so, former administrations cannot be criticized for the system under which they operated; the criticism should be levelled at the minister under whom the boards operated. The minister referred to the fact that these different boards consisted only of three men. The harbour boards cannot be blamed for not having sufficient staff to see that matters were looked after properly. This is another instance where the criticism should have been directed against the government for not providing additional help.
What is going to happen after this new central board has been set up? I understand there are to be three commissioners, one having a particular knowledge of finance, one being particularly interested in marine affairs and the other being an engineer. To me it would appear that the outstanding qualification for a chairman or member of this board

should be business training. Such a member should have experience in dealing with big business, because these ports are big business. Instead of an engineer, I would suggest a legal man. I have the port of Halifax particularly in mind in making this suggestion. The central board at Ottawa or Quebec, wherever it may be located, will have at its command the best of engineering ability. The personnel of this board should be considered in a very careful manner.
The minister referred to local contacts, and mention was made of what had happened in Vancouver. I think that is another reason why there should be local control, particularly in connection with Vancouver and Halifax. I believe someone in local control could make contacts to much better advantage than a person unfamiliar with the requirements on the Atlantic or the Pacific. Reference was made also to the accounting system, but that could have been taken care of under the old regime. I do not think that is a sound reason for establishing a central board. I think a uniform accounting system could have been set up quite easily.
I am a little apprehensive as to the future of the ports of Vancouver and Halifax under this proposed central board. I should like to repeat what the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) said "that no centralized control could replace the efficiency of active local administration or the special knowledge and initiative of the local business community, both of which are vital to the prosperity of a port." I leave that thought with the minister. I am dealing only with the principle of this bill and I do not intend to take up the particular clauses, as did the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). I agree with him when he says that they will have to receive very careful consideration when we are in committee.
I feel I should congratulate the minister upon bringing this bill before the house. I want to go on record as not being opposed to the abolition of the so-called three-men commissions, for I believe that just as much good can be derived from one-man port management as from three-men management. I am in favour of the bill, but I reserve my right to criticize certain sections at some future time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion too much money has been spent these past years in investigations. In many cases outside talent was brought in when it was not needed and in many instances the great expense incurred could not be justified. I want to commend

National Harbours Board-Mr. Gariepy
the minister for drawing something useful and something really important from the Gibb report. I do not know that I would have taken part in this debate had not the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) made a remark about two ports which in his opinion should be left out of the seven. I rise to make sure that one of those two is not the important port of Three Rivers.
Three Rivers is the best natural port in Canada. It is easy of access, no tugs being necessary. It has no tides and it compares favourably with Quebec and Montreal and even with ports situated on the shores of the oceans. The figures given to the house tonight by the minister disclose that the port of Three Rivers has been almost able to carry itself. The interest on the millions spent has been paid year after year as well as allowance for depreciation. There does not seem to have been any abuse in this case. This is why I was very careful to investigate the provisions of this bill and endeavour to see whether local sentiment would be taken care of and whether this was a move in the right direction. The hon. member for Mount Royal has mentioned that local sentiment might be against this measure, but I want to say that the people in my riding are prepared to give the principle of this bill a fair trial. There are many business men in the community who felt that they should have been recommended as members of the local harbour board. I am satisfied that there were many people who had ambitions in connection with the harbours, but such ambitions must be set aside.
In my opinion this measure is entitled to favourable consideration, especially when we are facing a financial crisis and an effort is being made to improve trade. In a country like ours trade and navigation should go together. I would say to the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Bertrand) that his argument appears to me to be not against but in favour of the measure. For how could the deepening of the St. Lawrence be done by the local harbour commission of Montreal? It would have to be done as a national undertaking. Our several ports can be developed only if they are nationally supported.
It is true that some local interests will have to be protected and it will be necessary to pay attention to the selection of the managers. For instance, I should regard it as bad business if the manager for Three Rivers were imported from Vancouver, though I like Vancouver. Vancouver is a large city, but the Vancouver mentality would not suit
Three Rivers, and Vancouver interests would object to a Three Rivers man being sent to direct the destinies of their harbour. I trust that the new board, with the help of the minister and the government, will see to it that great care is taken in making these appointments. The manager will have to be the link between the business interests and the board; he will not be independent; he will not rule as did the old commission. The managers will have vast powers, and I hope that in their selection the minister and the board will not lose sight of the remarks I make to-night.
I might mention in closing that the press of the country,, of both parties, has been supporting the principle of the measure. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George say that he did not object to the principle of the bill, but he made some remarks in connection with its details and I was surprised when he tried to give the impression that the preparation of the measure itself had not been up to the mark. For instance, he wants a detailed description of the properties. How can that be given? The new board simply takes over whatever assets the old boards possess. Property and civil rights do not come within the jurisdiction of the dominion; they are a matter of provincial legislation. There are questions of boundary, even in my own community; we are not quite sure where the boundary line runs. So that this bill could not define boundaries of the property that will be taken over. It is being accepted holus bolus as a going concern. The same applies to most of the criticism which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has offered.
The new board has capacity to sue and to be sued. It is a corporation which will pass bylaws and these have to be published in the Canada Gazette. They can be disallowed by the governor in council. As regards the financial provisions, there are several sections dealing with money matters, one following from another;, and they are all, it seems to me, in perfect accord. I say, therefore, that the minister deserves our support in the move he is making. He was not in public life before he came to this parliament, and he is bringing some trouble upon himself in this bold step. He has a vast department to administer, and I submit that it is up to us, no matter from what constituency or province we may come, to stand by him, because he is moving in the right direction. Boundary lines should not divide us. I have heard someone speak of east and west. I do not care; we are all Canadians and this

National Harbours Board-Mr. Bennett
bill is aimed at improving the position of our harbours. I think therefore it is my duty to support it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
There is in this bill no
principle that has not met with general approval. The bill does embody the general sense of the report made by Sir Alexander Gibb in 1932. From 1926 to 1930 I was an interested spectator in this house when estimates were from time to time made of the money necessary to be expended in the harbours of Canada. I saw the undertaking for the construction at Wolfe's cove commence. We all knew that this work should not be done, but it was. I saw the first appropriation made for Chicoutimi, which could not under any circumstances be justified; and I saw the harbour of Montreal saddled with the Montreal bridge, which involves a responsibility financially of $950,000 per annum that must now be paid by that harbour commission or by that harbour. All that we saw, and there are others to which I could refer, including obligations created in connection with the harbour of Halifax and obligations created in connection with the harbour of Saint John, which harbour for many years was of course administered by the people of that city, and which represented vast expenditures made by them of moneys obtained by them on their own credit. The construction of the Negro Point breakwater and the Courtenay bay undertakings referred to by Sir Alexander Gibb I remember from my childhood. The harbour of Montreal was, as I say, in the p'osition where certain works were being undertaken, and it was during those years saddled with the liability connected with the harbour bridge. The harbour of Vancouver came into being in its present condition in more recent years. Certain piers were constructed; others were in process of construction; a sinking fund had been accumulated and investments made, and as a matter of fact the sinking fund, instead of being expended for the purpose of acquiring securities issued by the harbour board itself, had been used for the purpose of buying various forms of securities, some of questionable value in the light of present conditions.
I made up my mind at the -time that this matter was of such importance to western Canada-and I was thinking then largely of western Canada-that it was necessary that there should be a complete investigation of the whole situation. I say western Canada because there is not a single bushel of wheat that is being shipped from western Canada that is not in some way affected by the ports through which it passes. It may be through

Churchill, and there we have expended vast sums of money upon which interest has been and must be paid. It may be through Vancouver, where vast sums amounting to millions of dollars have been expended, great properties purchased upon which docks have not yet been erected. Vast sums have been expended at Prince Rupert, which is not a port within the purview of this bill, and vast sums have also been expended in the eastern part of the country, all looking to one end. That end of course has been -the providing of facilities for the shipment out of Canada of goods produced in Canada and the entering into Canada of goods that are bought abroad.
We had hardly attained office after the first conference of 1930 when I began to look about for the purpose of determining where we could obtain a suitable engineer to make a report upon the whole harbour situation. Various names were suggested. We finally concluded that it was desirable to ask Sir Alexander Gibb, who had had great experience, to undertake the work. He said that he was willing to do so; he came to Canada, and those who are familiar with his report, to which some reference has been made to-night, will find that he refers to certain minutes of instruction which I gave to him on April 29, 1931, summarized in the following terms:
1.	To report upon the efficiency of existing facilities;
2.	To report upon the additional facilities required to take care of the increasing traffic of the -ports for a period of twenty-five to fifty years, keeping in mind the use to the maximum of existing facilities;
3.	To report on the best method of administration, whether through harbour commissioners or a department of government with a general manager, or otherwise, for the purpose of securing economy and efficiency, due regard being had to the fact that the moneys of the taxpayers of the whole of Canada will be used in -the development of the ports.
Under these three heads Sir Alexander Gibb's report deals with the situation as he found it. After having visited every port; after having examined at great length the documents and papers in various departments of the public service; after having talked over the matter very fully with the permanent officials and particularly with Mr. Alexander Johnston, to whose services he refers, [DOT]he made the report to which reference has been made this evening. In that report he dealt with the matter under two broad heads, first, that of administration, including for my purposes everything incidental to the administration of the port, and on the other hand he dealt with the condition of the several ports, analyzing the financial position and

National Harbours Board-Mr. Bennett
dealing with their future and the work that had to be done and was being done in those ports.
To deal for the moment with the question of administration, he arrived at certain definite conclusions. Those conclusions, in the main, are embodied in the legislation now before the house. There are one or two particulars in which it differs, and to those particulars I must direct attention either now or later, because some of them are of vital importance. In the second branch of his report, dealing with the facilities provided! by the several ports themselves, he had much to say that is of the greatest interest. I will not deal with that at length, but there are a few features of his report which I think could properly be placed upon Hansard, because it seems to me they are of considerable importance looking to the permanent value of this legislation and its importance in the economic and commercial life of this dominion. His very first words were these:
The ports of Canada, although they have a capital value of about $370,000,000 only, are part of a transportation system which, including railways, canals and roads, is assessed at $4,500,000,000 and constitutes over a seventh of the country's estimated wealth. The principal ports are not, as in many countries, founded on the service of a great exporting or consuming area in their immediate neighbourhood; nor have they been created and developed by merchant or shipping interests. They exist primarily as the connection between land and sea in the long route that the exports of Canada must take to reach their market; and for that reason, by the terms of confederation, and in distinction from the position in the United States where the ports have remained almost entirely in the control of individual states and cities, almost all ports in Canada have become federal property.
Then he deals with the average distance from Canadian ports to the points where imports and exports are dealt with, and speaks of it as five hundred miles, saying that in Great Britain it is only fifty miles. Leaving that for the moment, there are one or two important matters to which I think attention might be directed. He finds that political activities interfere greatly with the value of the ports. That is a matter with reference to which I am going to make some observations when this bill is in committee, but the danger of centralization lies in the fact that the local authorities may -be denuded of power and an effort madte to control and operate by the central power or authority. With distances so great the central power cannot possibly function. The other day there was a snowstorm in Montreal. The question of the removal of the snow was referred to Ottawa, as I am informed, and certain delays took place before the question was finally dealt with.

I only know that those who were charged with responsibility in that port so informed me. There is no reason why this should not be known, and there were certain delays. It is certain that in connection with the harbour of Vancouver the distance is too great to centralize here at Ottawa the administration of the port as such. Sir Alexander Gibb refers to that and makes his position extremely clear, pointing out what the difficulties are by reason of our great distances, and then goes on to indicate that there should be a more careful control over the financial side of these matters. I recall in this house, when the late Mr. Robb was Minister of Finance, having to deal with the question of the adequacy and sufficiency of the audits of harbour commission reports. It will be recalled that largely through the efforts which we made at that time Mr. Robb accepted the view that the auditor general should be charged with the responsibility and seized with full jurisdiction to investigate and audit the reports of the harbour commissioners of Canada, and it was the custom and habit to have that done under certain conditions to which I need not now refer. It was quite apparent that there was an inadequate accounting system, lacking in uniformity, in the various ports of this country. Sir Alexander Gibb refers to that with great particularity. He says:
I consider, therefore, that it is important there should be a close and continuous check by the central government. The form this control will take must depend on the administration system that is to be introduced. If the present arrangement continues, then the harbour supervisor's department should be strengthened and' the supervisor turned into something like a controller-general. if any other form of control be adopted, it must include its own controller, since I feel that even if the auditor general could carry out periodical inspections under the Audit Act, only a staff fully conversant with port operation is in a position to keep a complete check on the accounting in a port.
Then he proceeded further, dealing with questions at various ports, and as to how he conceived matters could be best dealt with. At page 22 I find this statement:
The ports should have no authority to raise funds independently, or to carry bank loans or overdrafts-other than an ordinary account or for ordinary operations.
Without traversing, as I might and) may hereafter have to do, the various paragraphs of the report, I want to deal at once with the question that I dare say suggests itself to the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches: Why, with this report before you, did you not proceed at once to give effect to it? You had this in 1932. During succeeding sessions ques-
1426	COMMONS
National Harbours Board-Mr. Bennett
tions were asked as to whether or not we were going to act upon the Gibb report, and in every instance the answer was that the matter was still under consideration. In this particular case that answer happened not only to be adequate but also to coincide with the exact fact. The reasons were two. The first was the condition that the government inherited with respect to work at the various ports. The second was that in the midst of that parliament I do not think I could have given effect to the report. I will put it in this way; I do not think the government could have carried this through in the midst of that parliament, I want to be perfectly frank about that, and the reason I congratulated the Prime Minister the other day upon dealing with this matter at that particular moment was because I believe that if he had not dealt with it at once on coming into office he could not have dealt with it at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
I gave these two reasons. Let us analyze them. First, go to Halifax. Does the house realize that the work in Halifax was not concluded on contracts that were given-I wish hon. gentlemen would take the trouble to look at the dates the contracts were awarded-for works that were not completed until December, 1934? I went down to the opening of pier B. We did, because of our financial position, endeavour to delay this work as much as possible; in fact one of the contractors did threaten litigation because he was not permitted to continue as rapidly as he would have liked. We had not the money. I desire the house to realize that most of the money that has gone into the ports of Canada has come from the consolidated revenue fund of this country, from collections that were made for superannuation purposes, for retirement purposes, from the Indian funds, from various funds that were not kept separate as trust accounts but paid into the consolidated revenue fund. That is another reason why this becomes so important. There was this work going on at Halifax. To take the harbour out of the control of the commission with the work partly done seemed an almost impossible task, and the engineers rather thought we should not do so. I think that probably is well known by everyone. I desire here to pay tribute to the two chairmen that I came into contact with in connection with the Halifax harbour, Mr. Phinney and Mr. Hether-ington. If ever two men were filled with a sense of civic pride and a desire to make a complete and finished job of the work in which they were engaged those two gentlemen

were. Mr. Phinney resigned in the middle of his term of office because his professional engagements prevented his continuing, and Mr. Hetherington took office as his successor. That work was not concluded until December, 1934. I give that reason why it was thought undesirable to change the control of the harbour at that time.
Then we come to Saint John. Saint John had two difficulties: First, the government of this country had assumed the obligation of the city of Saint John in connection with the construction of the harbour, and, second, there was great difficulty in connection with the construction of a cofferdam that had twice gone out with tremendous loss, so that the extras ultimately paid in respect of that work exceeded by something like one hundred per cent the amount of the original contract given to the Atlas Construction company. Anyone who has had to do with the construction of a cofferdam in tidal waters with a current of six to eight knots an hour will realize how difficult it is to construct a cofferdam and maintain it while the work is being carried on. But the works were finally completed, and I recall the opening of those docks. That was not until 1933, if I remember aright. It was thought-and I think properly so-and the opinion given us by those well able to judge was, that to interfere with the general scheme during the progress of the works was not desirable. But in addition to that, the harbour of Saint John suffered a great loss by reason of fire destroying three of its docks in the early part of that year. There were on the property certain sheds of doubtful value; there was wooden construction, and the fire completely devastated the docks in a very short time. At any rate the work at Saint John harbour was in such a state that to change the system of administration at that time seemed an almost impossible task. We directed our attention to two things, finishing the existing work, and trying to delay as long as possible the construction of the new docks, and when they were constructed to construct them of permanent material and to secure the best possible advice as to the character and type of construction that should be followed. I think the minister will agree that the idea of constructing concrete pillars upon which to erect the work was much to be preferred to some other suggestions that were made. At any rate the best engineers available reported in that sense.
Then let us consider the port of Quebec. Those interested in reading the details will take Sir Alexander Gibb's report. There you

National Harbours Board-Mr. Bennett
had a harbour built up from the very early years, and then a new dock system altogether at Wolfe's cove where the Canadian Pacific bored through the hill for the purpose of taking its trains through the tunnel. We constructed the new wharf and dock, wholly unnecessary and in no sense related to the old harbour works at the harbour of Quebec, as Sir Alexander Gibb pointed out. I am not going into the details of that, for I have no desire to engage in recriminations, but there was no justification for the work at Wolfe's cove. The very first thing that confronted us as a government was a partly completed work at Wolfe's cove which was being moved by lateral pressure straight into the St. Lawrence river. We had to deal with that and to expend money as it became necessary for the purpose of preserving that property and stopping that movement. I am happy to say that the means taken to effect the end desired proved successful and there has been no further movement into the river of that great dock by reason of the lateral pressure. It was a shed with two floors, as Sir Alexander Gibb says, but only one part of it has been used as yet. Any hon. member who has seen that vast shed knows how little it has been put to use in the service of the country. I recall when we voted $10,000,000 for the harbour of Quebec it was said by the responsible minister that it would be the last sum that would be asked; that no greater sum would be required. We all know that the work cost more than was intended, and finally, as Sir Alexander Gibb points out, in order to preserve the works at the lower harbour something had to be done to repair them. The government put the work off; we had not the money to spend. But when the property was falling into disrepair; when the concrete was going to pieces the report was that we must do something, and we spent there substantial sums of money to repair the old wharf and dock property at the harbour proper of Quebec.
Then we come down the river to Chicoutimi. Can any one explain why Chicoutimi harbour came into being at all? All one has to do is to look at it. It is only necessary to study the plan which we inherited, of the work which we had to continue, which I do not think is yet completed, to realize how difficult it is to understand why that work was launched. There is of course a great difference of opinion as to the ultimate selection of the place where the works now are and the place where it was thought they were being put. A picture postcard showing the ships loading at Ha I Ha! bay would leave the impression that the works were there, but as a matter of fact that is not where they are at all. Be that as it may, the completion of the contract in connection with Chicoutimi found that harbour in much the same position as those of Saint John and Halifax. To change the administration at that time was almost impossible.
We then come to Three Rivers. There again the work was partly done; there again the harbour board had undertaken certain responsibilities and carried out in part the work which they had contemplated. There again the top of the wharf was not floored; there again part had not been completed by proper ballasting to enable it to be made effective and efficient as a port facility, and so had to be extended or else what had been done was of no use. So the engineers undertook to complete it, and finally a revenue was secured from the International Paper Company in connection with the use of a certain part of that port.
Then we come to Sorel. Now, Sir Alexander Gibb points out that there are two kinds of ports, publicly owned ports, and privately owned ports or enterprises. He goes on to point out that there should not be conflict between the two. I shall not take time to-night to go into a detailed discussion, although I may have to read these paragraphs at a later time. They may be familiar to hon. members. But at that port there was a situation in which grain elevators were involved. He points out that competition for traffic and lower rates of privately owned companies had shattered the very value of the port that public money had created. And he said, what is more, that the privately owned business had selected the cream of the business, and had profited, leaving the publicly owned enterprise to take care of the unprofitable business.
The harbour at Quebec had expected a large grain business. It did not eventuate. The harbour of Montreal had constantly supplied facilities for shipping Canadian and American grain to the ports of the world. Sorel meant the loss to some extent of part of the traffic which Montreal had previously had. Sir Alexander Gibb deals with that point at some length. There again we had a position in which Montreal had partly finished work, but their general plan had for the moment been concluded, unless very large expenditures were undertaken dealing with the question of deepening the harbour, on the one hand, and the seaway or pathway to the sea, on the other. When we came into office the pathway, which perhaps might
1428	COMMONS
National Harbours Board-Mr. Bennett
more properly be called the seaway channel, was being developed to a depth of thirty-five feet. We continued that work. I believe any government in Canada would have done the same thing. I think they would have regarded it as their duty, and after a change of government that work was pushed forward with very great expedition indeed under the contract that bad been made. And there remained, according to the profile which I examined myself with care, a very small number of spots in which rock, gravel and other parts of earth had to be removed for the purpose of making the channel complete from the bridge that crosses the St. Lawrence, near Quebec, straight up to the harbour.
But the harbour itself had not been deepened to thirty-five feet. A certain school of engineering thought believed that fact meant a constant drain by the swift flowing current of water from the harbour, so that the harbour became less useful than otherwise. Down in the basin near Vickers it will be recalled that certain dredging had taken place, but it was pointed out that some of the vessels requiring a heavy draught of water, owing to the shortage of water in the river had to leave with smaller cargoes than they otherwise would have had.
So that as a result of careful study of the situation, and discussion of it with competent engineers Sir Alexander, I think, himself realized that the report would have to be made effective by legislation at the beginning of a new parliament. I believe if this government had not seized the opportunity on coming into office to do what was done, it would have been quite impossible to do it at all. I say that for two reasons. I have no desire in any sense to magnify the political viewpoints of one party or to minimize the advantages of another. In dealing with a matter of this kind it is quite fair to say that one has always desired to do exactly what the other did-used to the maximum for political purposes, consistent with the discharge of duties which rested upon them, the work which might take place in these various harbours. That meant political control in the worst, and not the best sense. There is nothing that gave me more concern than did the whole question of the harbours of this country, for the reason that the whole life of western Canada is bound up with them. They are deeply concerned in the tolls that were to be paid for the handling of freight through them, inward or outward.
We have not had anything to do with the development of the harbour at Toronto. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church)

very properly pointed out to-night that if hon. members want to see a really magnificent piece of work they should go and look at the work in Toronto. At that point there has been redeemed from the lake an area of land) now amounting to many acres. There has been established a breakwater outside, and within the lagoon there is still water. I would say that there is a waterfront and a boulevard second to none in any part of the country. Then, it is provided that in the eastern end there may be industrial development of oil refining plants, and works of various kinds. Again, the higher type of building necessary for manufacturing purposes we find not on the boulevard but distant from it, and between the main part of the city and the water. Hon. members would find that many new buildings have been erected in that area. Development of that kind is not possible in some of the other harbours, because they do not lend themselves to it. You cannot have it in Saint John harbour; you cannot have it in Halifax harbour. There is an area around the harbour which might be available if the old buildings were cleared off, but the development could not be done as it was done in Toronto. Neither would it be possible in Montreal, because the harbour railway must from very necessity operate at different points, and conditions would be different from those in Toronto.
In the city of Vancouver we had an added difficulty, a very great difficulty indeed. It is well that the house and the country should realize that at the entrance to the harbour there is a narrow passageway, followed by a narrower one called the second narrows. In days gone by across the second narrows a bridge was erected. The bridge had been struck by a vessel entering the narrows channel, with the result that injuries were sustained and the span ultimately dropped into the bottom of the harbour. Then it became necessary to construct a new bridge. Certain questions of legal liability arose. It will be observed that after the new span was erected limitations as to liability were imposed by the statute other than those which would be attached by the common law, under judgment of the privy council.
Therefore this work which the minister is now carrying on, or this legislation which the minister now submits to the house, was not dealt with for reasons which I shall no more than repeat: First, the condition of the work in the various harbours referred to, and, second, that I did not believe, nor do I yet believe, after discussing the matter -with my

National Harbours Board-Mr. Bennett
colleagues, that it was possible to introduce that legislation in the midst of a term of parliament.
We now have the bill before us. In the main it contains the recommendations of Sir Alexander Gibb with respect to the question of central control. But Sir Alexander pointed out that you had to determine certain legal questions before you went further. Shall this board of management-and I shall call it that for the sake of argument, although it is described in the bill as a national harbours board-be said to be an agent of the crown? It is a corporation. It is capable of suing and being sued. It is a corporation acting as an agent of the crown. Sir Alexander Gibb deals with the point and states that it is a matter of gravest moment, one which must be considered from many angles. As to what the legal position was I must not take time to read to-night. But as to what the legal position then was he is in doubt. He states that lawyers in Montreal have advised that the position is one way, and that the department has advised that it is another way. I submit that the bill in its present form must be amended not only along the lines suggested by my colleague, the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George, who has dealt with it in the light of his wide experience in matters of this kind, but from the legal implications which flow from the appointment by the crown of an agent.
Last year when the marketing bill was before the house the right hon. gentleman now leading the government raised a point, in connection with which he stated that he was not a lawyer. His point had to do with the appointment of an agent of the crown. The marketing board was not the crown; it was a separate organization. We have said in the bill that this national harbours board should be a corporation, and it is therefore to have continuing life. It may sue and be sued. But it is the agent of the crown. That is one of the points to which, as I say, Sir Alexander Gibb directs attention, and which I think is not adequately safeguarded in this bill. Must there be a petition of right to sue this board? I shall not repeat the arguments introduced by my friend and colleague from St. Lawrence-St. George, but shall leave the matter at that. But I do think this legislation must be reconsidered very carefully with respect to that angle.
Now we come to the next question, having set up a corporation as the agent of the crown. The question of a corporation being the agent of the crown is a modern doctrine. The question of a corporation acting as a trustee, as an executor, is also a modern development of practice. Although the three men composing the board are living entities, the result is an entity that does not live, and that is a corporation, not a corporation sole, but a corporation having continued existence and capable, as I say, of suing and being sued. That phase of the question I commend to the minister for most careful consideration, for I think he will find that under the decisions of the courts grave difficulties arise which must be overcome.
I shall not repeat the argument as to boundaries. The difficulty about this to which the minister has referred is not a difficulty that is not capable of solution. He has contented himself with saying that the boundaries of the harbours will continue to be the boundaries as they now are, and then says that as there are additions or otherwise there will be an extension or contraction of those boundaries. Having regard to the decisions of the privy council in connection with the harbour of Montreal, when the whole matter was litigated at great length as to the rights of riparian and other owners, and as to the right to the land under the water, which vitally affects the question of navigation as distinguished from the use of water for any other purpose, I believe there is a problem of first-rate importance which must receive more consideration than it has received in this bill.
There are several other questions which I should like to deal with, but which I may deal with at a later time because I have no desire to keep the house unduly long in further considering this bill. But there are problems in connection with expropriation. There are questions that arise in connection with the acute problem of ownership for purposes of taxation. No one knows better than, for instance, one member of the administration, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) of the difficulties that have arisen in connection with the development of taxation. The British North America Act declares that crown property is free from taxation, and neither the government nor any member of it nor the members of this house can violate the constitution and make property taxable. But the privy council held this, that the interest of lessees in properties may be taxed as distinct from the property itself, and so from time to time an effort has been made to tax the value of leases held by lessees of dockage and other space on wharves and properties owned by the various harbour commissions. This bill deals with that, not directly, but by implication. It says:
Any property now held by any of the corporations in the name of such corporation may continue so to be held until the same shall be transferred by such corporation or the board to His Majesty.
1430	COMMONS
National Harbours Board-Mr. Bennett
There is one of the most difficult and complex of all questions with which legal practitioners have to deal, so I suggest, in view of the efforts being made by municipalities from time to time to tax properties of this kind, that there should be in this bill a provision that beyond all peradventure vests these properties in the crown, and appropriate action should be taken to that end for that purpose. That should be done without delay. Then, once these properties are vested in the crown, the question of taxation disappears.
It might well be desirable in this measure to provide that nothing in this bill shall be taken in any sense to lessen the right of municipalities to tax the interests of lessees in these properties. We have had that question, of course, in connection with homesteads; we had it in connection with the old Canadian Pacific railway lands; we had it in the celebrated case that went from Saskatchewan, and we had it in the Calgary and Edmonton case that went from Alberta. These questions have been settled. But the	late government was
bothered with petitions claiming, for instance, that legislation about to be introduced into the legislature of British Columbia proposed to tax the interests of certain persons in properties that they held under lease, and that the basis of taxation was to be as though they owned the property. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre will recall that ultimately the legislation was withdrawn, because it was pointed out that the federal government could not concur in any such legislation as that being enacted. I suggest to the minister that it might be made abundantly clear, to remove any doubt, that nothing in the bill was intended in any sense to lessen the right of municipalities to tax the interest of lessees in properties under lease. Then the difficulties that have been experienced would disappear.
I think on the second reading I should point to one difficulty, and that is the power of expropriation. When the Canadian National Railways were dealing with Churchill, on the one hand, and the city of Montreal, on the other, the Minister of Railways filed a plan, and under the law as it stood, he being a minister of the crown, the property was expropriated. That meant that the property was taken from the owner and vested in the crown. The right of way for projected changes in Montreal in connection with the terminal was vested in the crown by the filing of a plan by the then Minister of Railways, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), I think. Now, this has been reenacted here, although it was the subject matter of much dispute and adjudication in the exchequer court. The bill says:

Any plan and description deposited under the provisions of the Expropriation Act shall be signed by one of the members on behalf of the board and the land so shown and' described shall thereupon be and become vested in His Majesty, unless-
So and so. The effect of that is for the crown to confer power upon three persons constituted a national harbours board, to expropriate properties in the name of the crown, and mark you, the plan may be signed by only one member of the board. I cannot think that a sound exercise of power, and I say that without any limitation at all. It has been in our law for many years with respect to certain railway proceedings. For instance, I recall that a Minister of Public Works was once able, by a plan being filed with his signature, to vest in the crown certain property requested for a post office site. Now you have this body, which is a body created by this parliament, which is the agent of the crown, empowered through the act of one member of the board to expropriate property and vest it in His Majesty. I think that is unsound. I mention that because an important principle is at stake there, a principle to which at least eminent lawyers in many countries have directed attention. One of the most, shall I say, powerful powers that the crown may exercise is that of compulsorily taking a man's property from him. In Churchill men for speculative purposes paid large sums of money for lots, and when the final determination took place they got in many cases a very much less sum than they paid for the lots. The property was taken compulsorily from them and it was said that any residue was to be given to Manitoba. I regarded that at the time, and still do, as an improper exercise of the powers of the crown. Here the crown is not exercising them; it is vesting them in a board, any one of whose agents may exercise that power. For any one member of a corporation to exercise the power conferred upon the corporation as an agent of the crown, I conceive to be greater power than ought to be exercised.
I shall not repeat what was said by my colleague, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, but there are in connection with this measure certain details that are of tremendous importance. These have to do with what might be called the administration of the funds of the enterprise. To create a trust fund has many advantages and to provide that it can be drawn from only under certain conditions is exceedingly wise. As a very young man I recall being told by an experienced man that one of the first things to do in dealing with a corporation is to provide that there must be two signatures on

National Harbours Board-Mr. Bennett
every cheque. One of the commendable provisions of our law is that trust funds that are held in trust for certain designated purposes must be used in a large sense for those purposes so that they may fall into the hands of persons who should subsequently receive them. It is a light thing to create a trust fund and say that the Minister of Finance may draw money out of it; it should be surrounded with many more safeguards than are provided in this bill. While a minister of the crown is free from personal responsibility, the privy council held in the case against Mr. Fulton of British Columbia that he as provincial secretary was liable because he had not done certain things that he might have done within the period of time at his disposal. I do not think the provisions of this measure deal sufficiently with the principles which, I believe, should prevail with respect to the segregation of funds for specific purposes.
We come now to one other principle which Sir Alexander Gibb said was of tremendous importance, that dealing with tolls and charges. I suppose that every hon. member knows of the reductions in elevator tolls which occurred in connection with grain for the purpose of securing more business for Quebec, on the one hand, and for other points between Quebec and Montreal, on the other. There are always those who are anxious to take advantage of such things. Sir Alexander points out the difficulties to be encountered in this connection. He points out how matters have been controlled in other countries to some extent and the necessity of dealing with them here. Those who are familiar with the litigation that took place in Montreal in connection with the habit of swapping wheat, so to speak, for the purpose of accommodating shippers will realize just what I mean when I say that it probably is desirable to see that the consent of the board should be received as to the adequacy of the security which may be taken in a place like Vancouver.
I get back to the principle in connection with which I desire finally to make an appeal to the minister. Apart from what has been said by my colleague, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I think the minister should give consideration to making some provision in this legislation with respect to tolls and charges so that there cannot be such a condition in competition between harbours as has prevailed heretofore. I am not sure that this bill does not improve matters to some extent, but I think they should be tightened up.
The next point I desire to leave with the minister is whether we have secured the autonomy of each port to the maximum, consistent with the exercise of general supervision by the central board. That is the whole issue. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Bertrand) is right; there must be autonomy in these ports. Sir Alexander Gibb points out that an engineer is a very bad man to have as a port manager. Sir Alexander occupies a distinguished position in his profession, and he said that he could not recommend that a port manager be an engineer. What the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) said a moment ago with respect to business men, I think is implied not only in the report of Sir Alexander Gibb but in this measure itself. I put it to the house and particularly to the minister: Must we not provide for the largest measure of autonomous control by the managers of these several ports? I say local government to the maximum, but subject to supervising power by this board with respect to everything that affects the national interest.
I do not think it is abundantly clear that these port authorities have sufficient, shall I say scope, to their activities to expect them to function successfully while, on the other hand, I am quite certain that the limitations and restrictions that by the bill have been imposed upon their activities in the national interest, having regard to the fact that the money is found by the people of Canada, are quite ample. I am satisfied of that but, if my memory serves me rightly, I said to Sir Alexander Gibb that I believed Canada with its great distances must be prepared to grant a large measure of self-government to the port authorities without parting with real control over finances, on the one hand, and general administration as signified by tolls and construction work, on the other.
Construction must be carried on with a view to the future, looking ahead twenty-five or fifty years. It must be carried on according to the most approved manner and so that it can be added to. It cannot be uniform for all ports. Consideration must be given to the flow of tide in Saint John, for example, or to the deep water in Halifax, where no dredging is required. Consideration must be given to the fact that you have borers abroad, such as in Vancouver, while you have none in Halifax. While there are no borers upon the river St. Lawrence, the life of timbers is not very long. These are all matters of variation, but the constant factor is a oneness in administrative practices, a oneness with respect to tolls and with respect to the principles that govern the application of tolls,
1432	COMMONS
National Harbours Board-Mr. Bennett
a oneness with respect to the financial structure and a oneness with respect to the conditions that must be imposed for the purpose of carrying on new works and undertakings so that these harbours, which are the property not of the government but of the people both east and west, in which the west has as great an interest as the east and in which the east has as great an interest as the west, may be national ports in the broadest and truest sense of the term.
There are ports in Canada which are not being dealt with by this bill. What is to become of them? How are they to be dealt with? What is to happen to New Westminster? It is not my purpose to discuss these matters at the moment, but I do say to the minister that if he will modify this legislation, not only in the manner indicated by my colleague, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, but also along the lines indicated by myself, that control while effective will not be such as to lessen the responsibility of those who have to look after the management of the port itself, and that consistent with the exercise of this control along the lines I have indicated there will be the largest possible measure of freedom, within limitations, on the part of those responsible for the administration of the port, that is, the management appointed under the statute.
There are references to Sir Alexander Gibb's report which I should like to have made, but in view of the lateness of the hour I have refrained, for which I am sure the house is deeply grateful. I am desirous of doing everything within my power to contribute my little towards making this bill as successful as it is possible to make it in operation so that it may reflect the earnest and deliberate desire on the part of the parliament of Canada to deal with the situation. That, I think, is of the first importance, because the minister has not yet signified whether the Montreal harbour bridge, for instance, is to be dealt with under this bill as part of the harbour. Our responsibility in that respect is so great; it extends over such a period of years, that it cannot be lessened or curtailed, and therefore it is important to know what will be done with respect to that harbour, which was self-sustaining before that load was placed upon it, before the period within which the contribution to be made by the province of Quebec on the one hand and the city of Montreal on the other, has passed away. That will expire in a limited time, and it is important to keep that fact in mind in dealing with the Montreal situation. There are other considerations to be borne in mind, special in their character, with

respect to each harbour, on which matters I shall have something to say when the house is in committee.
On motion of Mr. Finn the debate was adjourned.
